## Page 50

4. It is a matter of record that protests were held between
20.07.2026 and 25.07.2026 in Delhi and in different areas of the
applicant-States as well as other parts of the country in which
thousands of young students participated. As a sequel to these
protests, 13 FIRs, details whereof have been reproduced above, came
to be filed by the Delhi Police in different police stations.
Similarly, several FIRs, as reproduced above, were also filed in
different police stations across the applicant-States. 
5.   As a gesture of goodwill and to ensure that the subject FIRs
do not cause any prejudice to the young students who participated
in the peaceful protests, and also as an acknowledgement of the
fact that mere participation in the protests is not taken as an
offence under the penal laws, the Central Government and the
applicant-States have taken a conscious decision not to pursue the
above-enumerated FIRs registered against the protesters.
6. A further commitment has been made that if any other FIR is
found to have been registered with regard to the same incident(s),
as  mentioned  in  the  subject  FIRs,  the  Delhi  Police  or  the
applicant-States  shall  not  oppose  the  affected  party  seeking
similar relief from this Court, namely, the quashing of such FIRs.
Learned Solicitor General, on instructions, has further submitted
that no fresh FIR qua the incidents of protests between 20/07/2026
and 25/07/2026 shall be registered in Delhi or in any other part of
the country.
7. As already noted, the Delhi Police has, in its application,
carved out an exception with respect to 2873 individuals allegedly
16

## Page 51

having serious criminal antecedents as per the National Crime
Records Bureau database and who were prima  facie  reported to be
present at the protest site. It is averred that an investigation is
required to ascertain the commission of offences relating to (i)
bodily harm or (ii) destruction of public property. Accordingly,
the Delhi Police has sought leave of this Court to register a fresh
FIR only against these 2873 individuals and that too, in conformity
with the observations made by this Court in its order dated
03/08/2026, wherein it was clarified that no protection could be
afforded to persons having criminal antecedents of ‘grave and
heinous offences’.
8. It is in this backdrop that the applicants, namely, the Delhi
Police and the four States, have sought the invocation of the
powers of this Court under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash
the subject FIRs, as per the details given in paragraph 3,
reproduced above.
9. During the course of hearing, the learned Solicitor General of
India has fairly stated that there may be more FIRs in the States
and Union Territories other than the applicant-States pertaining to
the same incidents of protests. He has submitted that it may be
advisable to put an end to those FIRs too. He has accordingly
sought appropriate directions from this Court for the closure of
those FIRs as well.
10. As regards the grant of compensation to the families of the
victim students, who committed suicide in connection with the
National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) UG examination, 2026,
learned Solicitor General of India states that the students who
17

## Page 52

committed suicide would be situated in different parts of the
Country.  Accordingly,  there  has  to  be  a  pan-India  policy,
acceptable to the respective State Governments, for payment of
compensation to the families of such unfortunate students who
committed suicide in connection with NEET-UG examination, 2026. He
further states that the Central Government shall formulate a
policy/arrangement in consultation with the State Governments for
payment of compensation to the families of the students who
committed suicide in connection with NEET-UG examination, 2026
within 90 days and shall arrange to make the payment thereafter.
11. Meanwhile, Mr. Saurav Das, Co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta
Party (CJP), who is also present in Court, has made the following
statement:
“As Co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta Party, I want to
state that in view of the positive assurances of the
Government of India and the judicial sanctity bestowed
upon them today, and in view of the Order being passed
by this Hon’ble Court, the CJP deems it appropriate to
withdraw the call for the march on 5 th September and
looks forward to the compliance of today’s order.
I also thank the Court for this decision and the
learned counsels on both sides, Ms. Vrinda Grover and
the Solicitor General for their efforts.”
12. We have heard learned Solicitor General of India as well as
learned senior counsel/counsel for the parties and taken note of
the statement made by the Co-convenor of the CJP. In light of the
commitment made before us by all stakeholders involved, including
the Union of India, some of the State Governments and the Co-
18

## Page 53

convenor of the CJP, and most importantly, keeping in view the
future prospects of the young protesters, who bonafidely came to
participate in a peaceful protest to raise their voice in favour of
certain demands, we find it a fit case to invoke our powers under
Article 142 of the Constitution in order to do complete justice
between the parties.
13. Consequently, these applications are allowed in terms of the
following directions:
(i)  All  the  FIRs,  the  description  whereof  is  reproduced  in
paragraph 3 above, are hereby quashed along with any proceedings
arising therefrom.
(ii)  If there is any other FIR registered with respect to the same
incidents of protests between 20.07.2026 and 25.07.2026 in any of
the States/Union Territories, including non-applicant States/Union
Territories, which has not been formally brought to our notice, the
same shall not be pursued or investigated, and such FIRs shall be
taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes.
(iii)  No State/Union Territory shall register any fresh FIR in
relation  to  the  incident  of  protests  between  20.07.2026  and
25.07.2026, save and except as permitted hereinbelow.
(iv)  The Central Government/Delhi Police shall be at liberty to
register a fresh FIR with respect to the 2873 individuals as
described in paragraph 4 of its application. Needless to say that
such FIR shall be registered without prejudice to the rights of the
affected parties to take lawful recourse in accordance with law.
(v)  The Central Government, in consultation with the State
Governments/Union  Territories,  is  directed  to  formulate  the
19

## Page 54

policy/make  arrangement  on  a  pan-India  basis  for  payment  of
compensation to the families of the students who unfortunately
committed suicide in connection with the NEET-UG examination, 2026
within 90 days and shall arrange to make the payment without any
delay.  Such a policy or arrangement may then also be adopted by
all the State Governments and the Union Territories as a regular
mechanism of compensatory measures.  
14. In light of the aforesaid directions, we direct that both
sides shall honour the statements and commitments made before this
Court. We make it clear that invocation of the extraordinary powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution is subject to the condition
that both sides shall abide by the terms/understanding of mutual
settlement.
15. Since these directions are being issued in the peculiar facts
and circumstances of the case, the same shall not be taken as a
binding precedent.
16.  Before parting, we place on record our appreciation for the
Union of India, the applicant-States, the counsel appearing for the
Petitioner(s), and the leaders of the CJP for their constructive
and cooperative approach, which has ensured that the best interests
of the young students remain at the forefront and that their future
is duly protected and secured.

4. It is a matter of record that protests were held between
20.07.2026 and 25.07.2026 in Delhi and in different areas of the
applicant-States as well as other parts of the country in which
thousands of young students participated. As a sequel to these
protests, 13 FIRs, details whereof have been reproduced above, came
to be filed by the Delhi Police in different police stations.
Similarly, several FIRs, as reproduced above, were also filed in
different police stations across the applicant-States. 
5.   As a gesture of goodwill and to ensure that the subject FIRs
do not cause any prejudice to the young students who participated
in the peaceful protests, and also as an acknowledgement of the
fact that mere participation in the protests is not taken as an
offence under the penal laws, the Central Government and the
applicant-States have taken a conscious decision not to pursue the
above-enumerated FIRs registered against the protesters.
6. A further commitment has been made that if any other FIR is
found to have been registered with regard to the same incident(s),
as  mentioned  in  the  subject  FIRs,  the  Delhi  Police  or  the
applicant-States  shall  not  oppose  the  affected  party  seeking
similar relief from this Court, namely, the quashing of such FIRs.
Learned Solicitor General, on instructions, has further submitted
that no fresh FIR qua the incidents of protests between 20/07/2026
and 25/07/2026 shall be registered in Delhi or in any other part of
36

## Page 71

the country.
7. As already noted, the Delhi Police has, in its application,
carved out an exception with respect to 2873 individuals allegedly
having serious criminal antecedents as per the National Crime
Records Bureau database and who were prima  facie  reported to be
present at the protest site. It is averred that an investigation is
required to ascertain the commission of offences relating to (i)
bodily harm or (ii) destruction of public property. Accordingly,
the Delhi Police has sought leave of this Court to register a fresh
FIR only against these 2873 individuals and that too, in conformity
with the observations made by this Court in its order dated
03/08/2026, wherein it was clarified that no protection could be
afforded to persons having criminal antecedents of ‘grave and
heinous offences’.
8. It is in this backdrop that the applicants, namely, the Delhi
Police and the four States, have sought the invocation of the
powers of this Court under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash
the subject FIRs, as per the details given in paragraph 3,
reproduced above.
9. During the course of hearing, the learned Solicitor General of
India has fairly stated that there may be more FIRs in the States
and Union Territories other than the applicant-States pertaining to
the same incidents of protests. He has submitted that it may be
advisable to put an end to those FIRs too. He has accordingly
sought appropriate directions from this Court for the closure of
those FIRs as well.
10. As regards the grant of compensation to the families of the
37

## Page 72

victim students, who committed suicide in connection with the
National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) UG examination, 2026,
learned Solicitor General of India states that the students who
committed suicide would be situated in different parts of the
Country.  Accordingly,  there  has  to  be  a  pan-India  policy,
acceptable to the respective State Governments, for payment of
compensation to the families of such unfortunate students who
committed suicide in connection with NEET-UG examination, 2026. He
further states that the Central Government shall formulate a
policy/arrangement in consultation with the State Governments for
payment of compensation to the families of the students who
committed suicide in connection with NEET-UG examination, 2026
within 90 days and shall arrange to make the payment thereafter.
11. Meanwhile, Mr. Saurav Das, Co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta
Party (CJP), who is also present in Court, has made the following
statement:
“As Co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta Party, I want to
state that in view of the positive assurances of the
Government of India and the judicial sanctity bestowed
upon them today, and in view of the Order being passed
by this Hon’ble Court, the CJP deems it appropriate to
withdraw the call for the march on 5 th September and
looks forward to the compliance of today’s order.
I also thank the Court for this decision and the
learned counsels on both sides, Ms. Vrinda Grover and
the Solicitor General for their efforts.”
12. We have heard learned Solicitor General of India as well as
learned senior counsel/counsel for the parties and taken note of
38

## Page 73

the statement made by the Co-convenor of the CJP. In light of the
commitment made before us by all stakeholders involved, including
the Union of India, some of the State Governments and the Co-
convenor of the CJP, and most importantly, keeping in view the
future prospects of the young protesters, who bonafidely came to
participate in a peaceful protest to raise their voice in favour of
certain demands, we find it a fit case to invoke our powers under
Article 142 of the Constitution in order to do complete justice
between the parties.
13. Consequently, these applications are allowed in terms of the
following directions:
(i)  All  the  FIRs,  the  description  whereof  is  reproduced  in
paragraph 3 above, are hereby quashed along with any proceedings
arising therefrom.
(ii)  If there is any other FIR registered with respect to the same
incidents of protests between 20.07.2026 and 25.07.2026 in any of
the States/Union Territories, including non-applicant States/Union
Territories, which has not been formally brought to our notice, the
same shall not be pursued or investigated, and such FIRs shall be
taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes.
(iii)  No State/Union Territory shall register any fresh FIR in
relation  to  the  incident  of  protests  between  20.07.2026  and
25.07.2026, save and except as permitted hereinbelow.
(iv)  The Central Government/Delhi Police shall be at liberty to
register a fresh FIR with respect to the 2873 individuals as
described in paragraph 4 of its application. Needless to say that
such FIR shall be registered without prejudice to the rights of the
39

## Page 74

affected parties to take lawful recourse in accordance with law.
(v)  The Central Government, in consultation with the State
Governments/Union  Territories,  is  directed  to  formulate  the
policy/make  arrangement  on  a  pan-India  basis  for  payment  of
compensation to the families of the students who unfortunately
committed suicide in connection with the NEET-UG examination, 2026
within 90 days and shall arrange to make the payment without any
delay.  Such a policy or arrangement may then also be adopted by
all the State Governments and the Union Territories as a regular
mechanism of compensatory measures.  
14. In light of the aforesaid directions, we direct that both
sides shall honour the statements and commitments made before this
Court. We make it clear that invocation of the extraordinary powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution is subject to the condition
that both sides shall abide by the terms/understanding of mutual
settlement.
15. Since these directions are being issued in the peculiar facts
and circumstances of the case, the same shall not be taken as a
binding precedent.
16.  Before parting, we place on record our appreciation for the
Union of India, the applicant-States, the counsel appearing for the
Petitioner(s), and the leaders of the CJP for their constructive
and cooperative approach, which has ensured that the best interests
of the young students remain at the forefront and that their future
is duly protected and secured.

     O R D E R
1. Application(s)  for  substitution  is  allowed  after
condoning the delay and setting aside abatement, if any.
2. Application(s)  seeking  intervention/impleadment  are
allowed.
3. Leave granted.
4. State of Haryana is in appeals challenging the
order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court,
wherein challenge was laid to the constitutional validity of
Sections 3 and 4 of the Haryana (Abolition of Distinction of
Pay Scale between Technical and Non-Technical Posts) Act,
2014 (hereinafter referred to as the ‘2014 Act’). By the
aforesaid  provisions,  the  State  of  Haryana  sought  to
withdraw the benefit of the "technical pay scale" given to

## Page 121

7
the employees in terms of the Government instructions dated
30.03.1982,  23.08.1990;  26.07.1991  and  09.08.2010
retrospectively, in respect of the employees who were yet to
be granted such benefits. The proviso to Section 4 clarified
that the persons who had already been granted the benefits
of the "technical pay scale" under the said instructions or
by virtue of orders of the Court shall continue to draw
their pay in the "technical pay scales”.
5. It was the case of the Writ Petitioners before
the High Court that due to the enactment of Sections 3 and 4
of the 2014 Act and specifically, the proviso to Section 4
of the 2014 Act, the Writ Petitioners had been unfairly
discriminated against and the impugned provisions of the
2014 Act had created an anomaly whereby, the juniors of the
Writ Petitioners working on the same post received higher
pay  compared  to  their  seniors  due  to  the  fortuitous
circumstance of higher pay being granted to them at an
earlier point of time.
6. It was also the case of the Writ Petitioners
that in service jurisprudence, no junior is allowed to draw
higher pay compared to that of a senior and therefore, the
Writ Petitioners were also entitled to a ‘stepping up’ of
pay.
7. Initially, the State of Haryana promulgated the
Haryana (Abolition of Distinction of Pay Scale between
Technical  and  Non-Technical  Posts)  Ordinance  2013,
(hereinafter referred to as the "2013 Ordinance"), which was
later enacted as the 2014 Act. The said Act was notified

## Page 122

8
vide a Gazette Notification dated 11.03.2014 upon the assent
being granted by the Governor of the State of Haryana.
8. The  appellant-State  of  Haryana  defended  the
legislation  on  the  submission  that  the  prescribed
qualification for the post, as per the applicable rules, was
to  be  seen  and  not  the  qualification  of  the  persons
occupying the post. It was also argued that in certain
cases,  irrespective  of  their  qualifications,  the  Writ
Petitioners had been granted the benefit of the technical
pay scale, which should not have been granted.
9. It was also submitted by the State that to bring
all the employees at par under one pay-scale regime, the
State had brought the legislation, which does not violate
Article 14 of the Constitution of India, as it was intended
to make unequals as equals.
10. It was also the case of the appellant-State of
Haryana  that  Government  Orders  did  not  confer  any
indefeasible right to obtain a pay scale, which the State
sought to remedy by enacting Sections 3 and 4 of the 2014
Act.
11. Under the impugned judgment of the High Court,
it  was  observed  that  when  the  Writ  Petitioners  were
appointed/engaged,  there  was  no  technical  qualification
prescribed for the post to which they were appointed.
Therefore, the benefit of the Government instructions could
not be denied to them. However, by enacting Section 3 of the
2014 Act, the benefits that were given to the employees at

## Page 123

9
the time of appointment to a post which had no prescribed
qualification,  could  not  be  sought  to  be  taken  away.
Furthermore, employees with technical qualifications, as per
the Act, serving at a post which may not be on a technical
pay scale, would not be liable to have such benefit suddenly
withdrawn by enacting Sections 3 and 4 of the 2014 Act.
12. The  High  Court  has  also  opined  that  the
legislation has to be read as a whole and the doctrine of
Harmonious  Construction  evolved  by  way  of  judicial
pronouncement needs to be invoked.
13. Having said so, the High Court issued certain
directions in paragraph 96 of the judgment, which are
reproduced hereunder:
“(i)  The  legislative  competence  of  the  State
Government is not in dispute and therefore the
constitutional validity of Sections 3 and 4 of the
2014 Act is upheld.
(ii) However, Sections 3 and 4 of the 2014 Act will
be applicable prospectively from the date the 2013
Ordinance was notified on December 10, 2013 and
will be applicable qua the new recruits who were
appointed  to  the  posts  where  technical
qualifications have been prescribed as per Section
2(h).
(iii) The pay of the petitioners is required to be
“stepped up” at par with their juniors from the
date the petitioners were regularised in service.”
14. However, before issuing the above directions,
the High Court assigned reasons as to why Sections 3 and 4
of the 2014 Act are held  intra vires  as the same would
operate  only  for  the  new  entrants.  Without  expressly
observing that the High Court has read down the provisions

## Page 124

10
of Sections 3 and 4 of the 2014 Act to save them from being
unconstitutional on the touchstone of Article 14 of the
Constitution  of  India,  the  High  Court,  while  issuing
directions in paragraph 96, has saved the legislation so
that it operates prospectively only in respect of new
recruits and all such existing employees who are within the
sweep or the legal mischief of the legislation are brought
at par, so that a situation is avoided where juniors are
getting higher pay than their seniors while they possess the
same qualification and perform exactly similar nature of
duties.
15. In our considered view, the reasoning adopted by
the High Court, while declaring the legislation as  intra
vires and  at  the  same  time,  granting  the  benefit  of
‘stepping up’ to the employees who are getting lower pay
than their juniors, cannot be faulted with. 
16. At this stage, learned Attorney General of India
appearing for the State of Haryana would submit that the
directions  issued  in  paragraph  96.3  relating  to  the
‘stepping up’ of the pay of the Writ Petitioners at par with
their juniors from the date the Writ P etitioners were
regularised in service, would cause serious prejudice to the
State of Haryana, inasmuch as there are a huge number of
employees who would have to be paid higher pay as a result
of the ‘stepping up’ for which they are not entitled in law
particularly when the High Court has upheld the validity of
Sections 3 and 4 of the 2014 Act. According to learned
Attorney General, once the provisions have been held intra

## Page 125

11
vires, any direction for the ‘stepping up’ of the pay of the
Writ Petitioners would be self- contradictory. He would
further submit that as long as Sections 3 and 4 of the 2014
Act holds the field as valid piece of legislation, any
direction by the Writ Court contrary to the provisions
thereof is not permissible.
17. Learned Attorney General, however, would submit
that considering the plight of the employees who have not
been paid benefits under the subject Government instructions
when they were in force, the directions issued in paragraph
96.3 for the stepping up of the pay can be restricted to a
particular period.
18. Countering the submission of learned Attorney
General, learned counsel appearing for the respondents/ Writ
Petitioners would submit that there is no contradiction in
the directions issued in paragraph 96.3 of the impugned
order. According to them, the directions have been issued to
save the constitutional validity of the 2014 Act and,
therefore,  at  first  blush,  it  may  appear  to  be  a
contradiction, but the sum total of the legal effect of the
directions would be to save the legislation and not to issue
any contradictory directions.
19. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent(s)  would,
however, leave it to the Court to modify the directions
contained in paragraph 96.3 to be applicable from the date
which appears reasonable and lawful.
20. We are informed that there are more than 2,000
employees who would be benefited by the directions issued by

## Page 126

12
the High Court for the ‘stepping up’ of their pay. Many of
those affected employees, had preferred writ petitions even
before the impugned legislation was brought in, first by way
of an ordinance and thereafter when it was made an Act.
While some others had not preferred any writ petition but,
had filed representations before the competent authority of
the State Government. The High Court had directed that
‘stepping up’ at par with their juniors, shall be made from
the date the writ petitioners were regularized in service.
However, in our considered view, once the legislation has
been upheld, allowing ‘stepping up’ from a date prior to the
date of the legislation may not be permissible because, as
on the date of the legislation, all such employees who are
either entitled to the benefit of the earlier Gazette Orders
or have actually been granted benefit under the Gazette
Orders, have to be brought at par. Therefore, the most
suitable date for the ‘stepping up’ of the pay of the
employees who are getting less pay than their juniors, would
be the date when the 2014 Act was notified in the Official
Gazette.
21. Therefore,  we  hold  that  the  conclusion  in
paragraph 96.3 of the High Court shall be modified to read
as follows:
“the pay of the Writ Petitioners and all such
similarly placed employees be ‘stepped up’ at
par with their juniors from 11.03.2014, i.e.,
the date when the 2014 Act was notified in
the Official Gazette”.

## Page 127

13
22. The Writ Petitioners and the similarly placed
employees shall be paid the arrears calculated on the above
basis within a period of six months from today, in terms of
the directions issued by the High Court in its impugned
order.
23. In  respect  of  all  other  employees  who  were
similarly situated as the respondents but were not allowed
the benefit and have either retired or died prior to
11.03.2014, the benefit of ‘stepping up’ shall be made
available to them notionally so that their pension is
brought at par with all such employees who are entitled to
the benefit.
24. The  appeals  are  disposed  of  with  the  above
modification in the impugned order(s) passed by the High
Court.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. While issuing notice, this Court had directed the Registrar
General of all the High Courts to furnish the details of pending
trials in the cases of acid attack victims in their respective
jurisdictions.  It  was  thereafter  noted  in  our  order  dated
27.01.2026 that 17 High Courts had sent their responses, the
details whereof were also mentioned in the said order.
2. While directing the High Courts to expedite the conclusion of
trials in the acid attack cases, this Court also directed the State
Governments and the concerned authorities to consider and formulate
appropriate rehabilitation measures for victims of acid attacks.
Consequently, the State Legal Services Authorities were directed to
7

## Page 145

submit  a  report  with  respect  to  the  rehabilitation  schemes
implemented by them for the grant of compensation, rehabilitation
and medical aid to the victims of acid attack.
3. In addition, the States and Union Territories were directed to
furnish information with respect to (i) the reported incidents of
acid attacks in year-wise format; (ii) whether the charge-sheets in
those cases were filed; and (iii) the number of cases still pending
at the trial stage or at the appellate stage. 
4. Another  important  direction  issued  was  to  furnish  brief
particulars of each of the victims of the acid attacks with
reference to their academic qualifications, current employment
status, marital status, and the medical treatment needed by them,
including the expenditure incurred thereon by such victims.  
5. On  09.03.2026,  the  reports  received  from  various  State
Governments and the High Courts were taken note of. Similarly, the
reports sent by the State Legal Services Authorities regarding the
victim compensation schemes and rehabilitation schemes were also
briefly referred to, whereupon a show cause notice was issued to
the State Governments and Union Territories as to why a scheme for
rehabilitation through employment in Government or Government-
controlled sectors for victims of acid attacks should not be
directed to be formulated. The State Governments were further
directed to consider a proposal to pay an honorarium equivalent to
a subsistence allowance to victims of acid attacks.
6. Some of the States have filed compliance affidavits from time
to time. We request learned counsel for both sides, along with the
learned  Amicus  Curiae , to collate the information regarding the
8

## Page 146

above issues from the compliance affidavits filed by the State
Governments and the High Courts in a tabulated form, specifically
pointing out as to whether the State Governments have introduced
any  rehabilitation  scheme  which,  inter-alia,  ensures  social
security for the victims of acid attacks. Such schemes may be
widened  to  include  free  education  at  all  levels,  employment
prospects,  free  treatment,  honorarium  during  the  period  of
unemployment, etc.  
7. Since it is not discernible from the compliance affidavit(s)
as to whether such schemes are in force, we direct all the State
Governments and the Union Territories to specifically formulate a
scheme in this regard and place the same on record within six
weeks.
8. The Union of India may also consider the desirability of
circulating a model scheme, along with a provision of necessary
assistance to the State Governments, to give effect to the above-
proposed scheme.  
9. The other challenge highlighted before this Court pertains to
the retail sale of the acid in the market. We are informed that
some guidelines were laid down in the year 2013, which have more or
less become obsolete and are not being followed. That being so, we
direct the Union of India to submit its response as to why a
complete ban on the retail sale of acid should not be imposed, or
in the alternative, why such sale should not be permitted in a very
restricted manner. Let such response be filed within six weeks.  
10. It is made clear that appropriate directions in this regard
shall be issued by us on the next date of hearing.
9

## Page 147

11. The NGOs that have come forward to assist this Court may also
submit their suggestions/recommendations, especially with respect
to any additional material that ought to be introduced in the
curriculum at the school and college levels for spreading awareness
regarding  preventative  measures  as  well  as  the  post-accident
treatments which are required on an emergency basis. Let such
suggestions also be placed on record within six weeks.
12. Post this matter for further consideration on 27.10.2026.

ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

General of all the High Courts to furnish the details of pending
trials in the cases of acid attack victims in their respective
jurisdictions.  It  was  thereafter  noted  in  our  order  dated
27.01.2026 that 17 High Courts had sent their responses, the
details whereof were also mentioned in the said order.
5. While directing the High Courts to expedite the conclusion of
trials in the acid attack cases, this Court also directed the State
Governments and the concerned authorities to consider and formulate
appropriate rehabilitation measures for victims of acid attacks.
Consequently, the State Legal Services Authorities were directed to
submit  a  report  with  respect  to  the  rehabilitation  schemes
implemented by them for the grant of compensation, rehabilitation
and medical aid to the victims of acid attack.
6. In addition, the States and Union Territories were directed to
furnish information with respect to (i) the reported incidents of
acid attacks in year-wise format; (ii) whether the charge-sheets in
those cases were filed; and (iii) the number of cases still pending
at the trial stage or at the appellate stage. 
7. Another  important  direction  issued  was  to  furnish  brief
particulars of each of the victims of the acid attacks with
reference to their academic qualifications, current employment
status, marital status, and the medical treatment needed by them,
including the expenditure incurred thereon by such victims.  
8. On  09.03.2026,  the  reports  received  from  various  State
18

## Page 156

Governments and the High Courts were taken note of. Similarly, the
reports sent by the State Legal Services Authorities regarding the
victim compensation schemes and rehabilitation schemes were also
briefly referred to, whereupon a show cause notice was issued to
the State Governments and Union Territories as to why a scheme for
rehabilitation through employment in Government or Government-
controlled sectors for victims of acid attacks should not be
directed to be formulated. The State Governments were further
directed to consider a proposal to pay an honorarium equivalent to
a subsistence allowance to victims of acid attacks.
9. Some of the States have filed compliance affidavits from time
to time. We request learned counsel for both sides, along with the
learned  Amicus  Curiae , to collate the information regarding the
above issues from the compliance affidavits filed by the State
Governments and the High Courts in a tabulated form, specifically
pointing out as to whether the State Governments have introduced
any  rehabilitation  scheme  which,  inter-alia,  ensures  social
security for the victims of acid attacks. Such schemes may be
widened  to  include  free  education  at  all  levels,  employment
prospects,  free  treatment,  honorarium  during  the  period  of
unemployment, etc.  
10. Since it is not discernible from the compliance affidavit(s)
as to whether such schemes are in force, we direct all the State
Governments and the Union Territories to specifically formulate a
scheme in this regard and place the same on record within six
weeks.
11. The Union of India may also consider the desirability of
19

## Page 157

circulating a model scheme, along with a provision of necessary
assistance to the State Governments, to give effect to the above-
proposed scheme.  
12. The other challenge highlighted before this Court pertains to
the retail sale of the acid in the market. We are informed that
some guidelines were laid down in the year 2013, which have more or
less become obsolete and are not being followed. That being so, we
direct the Union of India to submit its response as to why a
complete ban on the retail sale of acid should not be imposed, or
in the alternative, why such sale should not be permitted in a very
restricted manner. Let such response be filed within six weeks.  
13. It is made clear that appropriate directions in this regard
shall be issued by us on the next date of hearing.
14. The NGOs that have come forward to assist this Court may also
submit their suggestions/recommendations, especially with respect
to any additional material that ought to be introduced in the
curriculum at the school and college levels for spreading awareness
regarding  preventative  measures  as  well  as  the  post-accident
treatments which are required on an emergency basis. Let such
suggestions also be placed on record within six weeks.
15. Post this matter for further consideration on 27.10.2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION (CIVIL)  NO.281 OF 2025
 RIYA                                        PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
RAJAN KUMAR             RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R 
1. The matter was taken up today in the Committee Room. 
2. Parties are personally present with their respective
counsel.
3. By our last order dated 26.5.2026, we had directed
the parties to appear before Ms. Nandini Gore, the learned
1

## Page 189

counsel and a senior Mediator for the purpose of exploring
the possibility of reconciliation and also for providing
visitation  rights  to  Riya  so  far  as  Khrishnavi  is
concerned.
4. The parties have been able to reach to an amicable
settlement before the Supreme Court Mediation Centre.
5. The Settlement Agreement dated 25.08.2026 has been
reduced into writing duly signed by the parties, their
respective counsel including the learned Mediator.
6. The Settlement Agreement reads thus:-
“SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT
This Settlement Agreement is entered into between Petitioner-
Ms. Riya W/o Mr. Rajan Kumar, D/o Sh. Darshan Singh R/o
Gobind  Nagar,  Phase-2,  Kahnuwan  Road  Batala , opposite
Kalgidhar Gurudwara, District Gurdaspar, Punjab (here in
after referred to as Petitioner-Wife/ First Party) and Mr.
Rajan Kumar S/o Sh. Mohinder Lal R/o Dablehad Road near
Khambi, District R.S Pura, J&K here in after referred to as
Respondent-Husband/ Second Party).
1. WHEREAS marriage between the Parties was solemnized on
19th August, 2022 according to Hindu rites and ceremonies
rights at Kartar Villa, Umarpura Bye Pass Road, Batala. The
2

## Page 190

Parties to the marriage are governed by the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1955. After the marriage Parties resided together at
Dablehad Road near Khambi, District R.S Pura and there one
female child namely "KHRISHNAVI JOJRA" out of this wedlock.
2. WHEREAS the Petitioner and Respondent have agreed to
dissolve their marriage by mutual consent in accordance with
law provides U/s 13 (B) of the Hindu Marriage Act.
3.  AND  WHEREAS  the  Parties  had  earlier  arrived  at  a
Settlement  Agreement  before  the  Supreme  Court  Mediation
Centre dated 10.01.2026. The settlement Agreement was filed
before the Hon'ble Court along with an application under
Article 142 Constitution of India, seeking a decree of mutual
divorce. On having perused the Settlement Agreement dated
10.01.2026 in its entirety, the Hon'ble Supreme Court opined
that Clause 3(vi) thereof, extinguished the Petitioner/Wife's
visitation rights of the child, even though the Petitioner
had voluntarily given up the same during mediation. The terms
of the Agreement being not acceptable, the Hon'ble Court
directed the Parties to remain physically present before the
Hon'ble Court on 06.05.2026 and accordingly the matter was
taken up in chamber/committee room (Supreme Court premises)
on the said date. After the Hon'ble Judges met the Parties
and the counsels, a detailed order was passed. The relevant
paras of the aforesaid order dated 06.05.2026 are reproduced
as under:
 "4. After talking to Riya and Rajan, we have reached to a
prima facie conclusion that as such there are no serious
disputes between the Parties. It is only on account of some
3

## Page 191

misunderstandings on petty issues that Riya parted with
Rajan.
It is true that the Parties reached to some consensus before
the Mediation Centre and the Settlement Agreement has also
been reduced into writing, but after speaking to Riya and
Rajan, we outright reject the settlement agreement.
5.  We want the Parties to go back before a seasoned
Mediator. We direct the Parties to appear before Ms. Nandini
Gore, the learned counsel and a senior mediator, for the
purpose of exploring the possibility of reconciliation and
also for providing visitation rights to Riya so far as
Krishanvi is concerned."
4.AND WHEREAS, pursuant to the aforesaid Orders, Ms. Nandini
Gore, a Senior Mediator, was appointed afresh for exploring
the possibility of reconciliation between the Parties and, in
any event, for providing visitation rights to the Wife (First
Party)  with  respect  to  the  minor  daughter,  "KHRISHNAVI
JOJRA", and mediation sessions were accordingly held between
the Parties before the said Mediator through virtual mode.
5. AND WHEREAS, in the course of the said mediation, the Wife
(First Party) met the minor daughter, "KHRISHNAVI JOJRA", on
two occasions through video call one of which was the
birthday  of  the  minor  daughter  "KHRISHNAVI  JOJRA"  and
thereafter met her physically on 21st August, 2026 at Comfort
Inn  Coral  River  Resort,  Pathankot,  Punjab.
4

## Page 192

6. NOW THEREFORE, in compliance with and pursuant to the
aforesaid directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India,
and keeping in view the welfare of the minor daughter,
"KHRISHNAVI JOJRA", it is agreed between the Parties the
following terms conditions:
i. That the Husband (Second Party) shall pay to the Wife
(First Party) a total sum of Rs. 8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight
Lakhs only) by way of RTGS transfer into the bank account of
the Wife (First Party). Out of the said amount, a sum of Rs.
4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs only) shall be paid on or
before the next date of hearing, i.e., 25th August, 2026,
before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, and the balance
sum of Rs. 4,00,000/- (Rupees Four Lakhs only) shall be paid
at the time when the final judgment/order/decree of divorce
is  passed  by  the  Hon'ble  Court.
ii. That the Husband (Second Party) shall pay Rs. 10,000/- to
the Wife (First Party) by way of UPI transfer, to withdraw
her  duplicate  documents  ie.  10th  class  Mark  Sheet  and
Certificate, 12th class Mark Sheet and Certificate, Degree
and Mark Sheet of Graduation and Mark Sheet and Degree of
Post Graduation or Diploma Certificate on the day of divorce
decree.
iii. That the Husband (Second Party) shall return her goods
(A) One Diamond Ring (B) A Pair of Silver Anklets (C) First
Party's Clothes, Purse, Sandal and other goods whichever
available with husband (second party) to the wife (First
Party).
5

## Page 193

iv. That the wife (First Party) shall return the earrings
which was given to the sister of the wife (First Party) by

v. That the Parties shall mutually decide a convenient place
for the exchange of belongings mentioned hereinabove. An
inventory of all items so exchanged shall be prepared in
writing and shall be signed by both Parties in token of

vi. That if documents of the Wife (First Party) ie. the 10th

7. The original settlement agreement is ordered to be
taken on record and the same shall be kept with the record
of this case.
8. What we have been able to gather from the settlement
agreement, insofar as the visitation rights is concerned,
is that the petitioner mother will communicate with her
daughter through assisted Video calls on Sundays and mother
petitioner would visit Khrishnavi once in three months.
9. We must clarify that Khrishnavi is residing with her
father in Jammu.
10. The  petitioner  is  residing  in  Batala,  State  of
Punjab.  Although  the  parties  have  reached  to  this
understanding  yet  we  clarify  that  insofar  as  mother
visiting  Khrishnavi is  concerned,  may  not  be  strictly
restricted to video calls on Sundays and travelling to
Jammu and meeting her in person once in three months. 
11. It is u nderstood and we have made ourselves clear
before the parties including their respective counsel that
10

## Page 198

as and when mother wants to visit Jammu to meet Krishnavi,
it shall be open for her to do so and the phone calls need
not be restricted just to one particular Sunday. As and
when mother would desire to speak to Khrishnavi, it s hall
be open for her to call her up including video calls and
also to visit Jammu any time.
12. It is needless to say that for the happiness of
Khrishnavi both father and mother should celebrate her
birthday together. 
13. In view of the aforesaid, all proceedings between the
parties stand terminated. 
14. All other obligations in accordance with the terms of
the settlement have been discharged.
15. We are informed that out of Rs.8,00,000/- (Rupees
Eight lakh only) to be paid by the husband to his wife.
Rs. 4,00,000/- (Rupees Four lakh only) has already been
transferred.
16. The balance amount of Rs.4 lakh shall be transferred
to the account of the wife by RTGS today itself.

## Page 199

17. In view of the aforesaid, the marriage solemnized
between the parties stand dissolved in exercise of our
jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution.

conditions of the Settlement Agreement.

20. We place our gratitude to Ms. Nandini Gore for
taking lot of pains in bringing around the settlement
between the parties.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.244 OF 2017
STATE OF UTTARAKHAND                          APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
MOHD. IRFAN                                 RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This appeal is by the State impugning the judgment
and order of the High Court1 dated 06.03.2014 whereby
Criminal  Appeal  No.80  of  2012  filed  by  the
respondent Mohd. Irfan (accused - husband of the
deceased)  was  allowed  and  his  conviction  and
sentence  under  Section  302  IPC  awarded  by  the
Sessions  Court,  Nainital,  vide order  dated
20.03.2012 in Sessions Trial No.118 of 2006, was set
aside. 
2. The  respondent  was  tried  for  offence  punishable
under Section 306 IPC with an alternative charge of
offence punishable under Section 302 IPC. The Trial
Court convicted and sentenced the respondent under
Section  302  IPC  and  sentenced  him  to  suffer
imprisonment for life.
3. While convicting the respondent, the Trial Court,
11 The High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital
1

## Page 215

inter  alia,  took  into  consideration  the  autopsy
report, proved by the doctor (PW-3), and testimony
of an eyewitness Mohd. Nizam (PW-2) i.e., minor
brother of the deceased who, at the time of the
incident, was staying in the house of the deceased.
4. The relevant facts regarding which there was no
serious dispute are culled out in paragraph 22 of
the  Trial  Court’s  judgment.  Paragraph  12  is
reproduced below:
"22- (i) It is uncontroverted that at the
time of her death, she was with her husband
in her matrimonial house. 
(ii) It was her second marriage with the
present accused Irfan in the year 1998 and
earlier to that she was married with another
person in Rampur. 
(iii) She had four children by first wedlock
and these children were with her ex-husband. 
(iv) By the present second wedlock she gave
birth to three children and deceased Shamim
Jahan  was  living  with  her  husband,  the
present  accused  Irfan  and  family  members
including children, in the town Kaladhungi,
District Nainital. 
(v) The period of second wedlock was about 9
years when she died. 
(vi) It is also an admitted fact that cause
of death was unnatural and cause of death is
shown anti-mortem hanging.
(vii) One external injury was also found in
the body of deceased Shamim Jahan upon her
2

## Page 216

examination during postmortem. 
(viii) It is also not disputed that the
accused had neither informed police, nor to
her parents but her dead body was brought
down from the place of hanging and was kept
out of the room in a cot in outer portion of
his house at ground floor. She was unbound
from her neck and the hanging material i.e.
scarfs (dupattas) were recovered from the
place of occurrence."
5. Paragraph 14 of Trial Court’s judgment records the
post-mortem details of the cadaver, as proved by the
doctor (PW-3). For ready reference, paragraph 14 of
the Trial Court’s judgment is reproduced below:
"14- Prosecution witness Dr. C.P. Bhaisora
(P.W. 3) has stated in his examination-in-
chief that on 22.03.06 he was posted in
Medical College, Haldwani as Asstt. Professor
Forensic Medicine. The dead body of deceased
Smt. Shamim Jahan was brought by police of
P.S. Kalaghungi. He conducted the postmortem
of deceased Smt. Shamim on 22.03.06 at 1:00
p.m. and prepared report as under: 
External Examination: Cyanosis was present
over fingertips of both hands, lips and both
ear lobules. Rigor mortis was present all
over the body with mild decomposition. Both
eyes  were  congested  and  pupils  dilated.
Blood-tinged  froth  was  present  over  both
nostrils.
Ante-mortem  injuries:  (i)  Blunt
contusion_of_size 4 x 3 cm present over back
and chest on left side 3 cm. below from the
3

## Page 217

lower end of left scapular.
(ii) Ligature mark over neck oblique, non-
continuous placed above the thyroid cartilage
in front of the neck, base of the ligature
mark was parchment like and abraded at places
length of the ligature mark was 20  cm and
2cm. width starting 2 cm. below from the
angle of left mandible reaching up to the
side of the neck over right side up to 2cm.
behind and right from the lower end of right
ear lobule after that there is a gap because
of hair over back on cut section of ligature
mark  at  places  a  dry  whitish  glistening
appearance present.
Internal  Examination:  Congested  and  small
hemorrhage  spot  present  over  meanings  at
place. 
Congested  and  hemorrhage  spot  present  at
places and proved the postmortem report as
exhibit ka-2."
6. Upon consideration of the evidence including the
testimony of PW-2 and the autopsy report which,
inter alia, revealed presence of blunt contusion of
size 4 cm X 3 cm over back and chest on left side, 3
cm below from the lower end of scapular, the Trial
Court convicted and sentenced the respondent on the
alternative  charge  of  offence  punishable  under
Section 302 IPC.
7. Aggrieved by the judgment and order of the trial
court,  the  respondent  preferred  Criminal  Appeal
before the High Court. The High Court by a cryptic
4

## Page 218

judgment allowed the appeal. To pinpoint the error
in  the  order  of  the  High  Court,  we  deem  it
appropriate to reproduce the entire 3 paragraphs
judgment of the High Court below:
"1.  Appellant  has  been  convicted  for  an
offence punishable under Section 302 of IPC.
Appellant was arraigned for trial in respect
of the charges as were framed, which are
punishable under Sections 306 of IPC and
Section 3 / 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
Appellant denied the charges. Trial commenced
when the prosecution witnesses were examined.
The last of the prosecution witnesses was
examined on 30th September 2011. Subsequent
thereto,  on  31st  January  2012,  a
supplementary charge in respect of  offence
punishable  under  Section  302  of  IPC  was
framed. In support of the said charge, the
prosecution  did  not  bring  on  record  any
evidence.  Appellant  was  examined  under
Section 313 of IPC once on 3rd August 2011
and subsequently, after framing of additional
charge on 15th February 2012. Appellant, in
course of recording statement under Section
313 of the Code, denied all allegations that
were put by the prosecution witnesses. Thus,
the trial stood concluded. After the trial
stood concluded, by the judgment, appellant
has  been  exonerated  of  the  charge  under
Section 306 of IPC as well as the charge
under Section 3 / 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act,
1961, but has been convicted for an offence
punishable under Section 302 of IPC without
5

## Page 219

there being one single evidence in support of
the said charge. 
2. We, accordingly, allow the Appeal, set
aside the judgment and order under Appeal.
Appellant is in Jail. He is directed to be
released forthwith. 
3. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the
Court  below  along  with  the  lower  court
records."
8. Questioning the impugned judgment and order, the
submission on behalf of the State is that the High
Court has proceeded to allow the appeal principally
on the ground that the Trial Court had acquitted the
accused of the charges punishable under Section 3/4
of Dowry Prohibition Act and Section 306 IPC and
therefore, as there exists no evidence of homicide
so as to convict the accused under Section 302 IPC,
there is no option but to allow the appeal and
acquit the respondent. 
9. It  has  been  submitted  that  the  High  Court  has
wrongly  observed  that  the  accused  was  acquitted
under Section 306 IPC. Accused was not convicted
under Section 306 IPC. The fact is that because he
was convicted under Section 302 IPC, which is a
graver offence, he could not have been convicted
under Section 306 IPC. The High Court overlooked the
provisions of Sections 221 and 386 of the Code of
6

## Page 220

Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short, CrPC) which
enables  the  Court,  firstly,  to  frame  alternate
charge(s), secondly, to convict the accused for the
offence  ultimately  found  committed  and,  thirdly,
empowers of the appellate Court, in an appeal from a
conviction,  to  alter  the  finding,  maintain  the
sentence or to alter the finding as well as the
sentence. It has been submitted that the evidence
led  before  the  trial  Court  indicated  that  the
deceased was harassed, and assaulted soon before her
death, which was corroborated by autopsy report.
Thus, even assuming that the charge of murder was
not substantiated, considering the nature of the
evidence on record, the appellate Court could have
altered the conviction and punished the respondent
for lesser offence including one under Section 306
IPC.
10. Accordingly, the submission on behalf of the State
is that the matter be remanded to the High Court for
a fresh consideration of the appeal. 
11. Per contra, the learned counsel for the respondent
submits  that  the  evidence  on  record  is  not
sufficient to convict the respondent-accused either
under Section 302 or under Section 306 IPC. He,
however, admits that the manner in which the High
7

## Page 221

Court has disposed of the criminal appeal cannot be
countenanced  and,  therefore,  a  remand  would  be
appropriate.
12. We have considered the rival submissions and have
perused the record carefully.
13. A perusal of the trial court judgment would indicate
that it is not a case of no evidence. PW-2, an
eyewitness, has deposed that the deceased was beaten
and an effort to strangulate her was made on the
fateful day. Whether his testimony is to be accepted
or not is in the realm of appreciation of evidence
which the High Court being an appellate court was
required to undertake, but it did not.  
14. The High Court allowed the appeal on the wrong
assumption  that  the  trial  court  acquitted  the
accused of the charge of an offence punishable under
Section 306 IPC. Here, the High Court overlooked the
provisions of Section 221 of CrPC which enables
court  to  frame  charges  in  the  alternative  and
convict a person for the offence which, in its
opinion was committed. Mere conviction of an accused
for a graver charge does not result in acquittal
from a lesser charge. The trial court did not acquit
the accused of an offence punishable under Section
306 IPC. Rather, it convicted the accused for a
serious offence punishable under Section 302. Once
8

## Page 222

the trial court took a decision to convict him under
Section 302 IPC, which was the alternate charge, it
could not have convicted him under Section 302 IPC.
But  on  an  appeal  if  the  High  Court  had  found
evidence to convict him under Section 306 IPC, it
could have acquitted him under Section 302 IPC and
punished him under Section 306 IPC if the evidence
so warranted.   
15. In  this  regard,  the  High  Court  overlooked  the
provisions of Section 386 of CrPC. Section 386 CrPC
provides that in an appeal from a conviction, the
appellate Court, which, in the instant case, would
be the High Court, has the power to: (a) reverse the
finding and sentence and acquit or discharge the
accused, or order him to be re-tried by a court of
competent  jurisdiction;  (b)  alter  the  finding,
maintain  the  sentence;  or  (c)  with  or  without
altering  the  finding,  alter  the  nature  or  the
extent, or the nature and extent, of the sentence,
but not so as to enhance the same. In our view,
therefore, the High Court was under an obligation to
peruse  the  evidence  and,  based  on  its  own
appreciation of evidence, decide whether the accused
– appellant before it – was liable to be convicted
under Section 302 IPC or under Section 306 IPC or
9

## Page 223

any lesser offence.  
16. In the instant case, the High Court failed to even
advert to the evidence brought on record. In our
view,  such  a  perfunctory  disposal  of  regular
criminal  appeal  against  conviction  cannot  be
countenanced. Here, the respondent was tried for
offence punishable under Section 306 IPC and in the
alternative for an offence punishable under Section
302 IPC. The trial court did not acquit the accused
under Section 306 IPC rather it convicted him for a
graver offence punishable under Section 302 IPC;
therefore, if the charge under Section 302 was not
substantiated, there were no fetters on the power of
the High Court to convict him for a lesser offence
including one punishable under Section 306 IPC, if
the evidence so warranted. 
17. In these circumstances, the High Court must decide
the appeal afresh bearing in mind the provisions of
Section 386 CrPC. We make it clear that since the
High  Court  had  not  discussed  the  prosecution
evidence, we are not expressing any opinion whether
the  respondent  is  liable  to  be  convicted  under
Section 302 or 306 IPC or for that matter any other
offence. 
18. Resultantly, the appeal is allowed. The impugned
order of the High Court is set aside. Criminal
10

## Page 224

Appeal  No.80/2012  filed  by  the  respondent  shall
stand restored on the file of the High Court. The
High Court shall consider and decide the appeal
afresh  in  accordance  with  law  without  being
prejudiced by any observations if any made by us on
the merits of the charge(s). 
19. The records which were called for from the High
Court shall be sent back within two weeks from
today. 
20. The respondent shall surrender/ appear before the
High Court on 30.09.2026. It shall be open for the
High Court to consider his prayer for suspension of
sentence as well as for bail pending consideration
of the appeal by the High Court.
21. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).             OF 2026

MANISH KUMAR                                                          ...APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR                                         …RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R 
1. Heard. Leave Granted.
2. The Appellant was arraigned as an accused in FIR No. 297 of 2025
registered for the offences punishable under Sections 191(1), 191(2), 190,
126(2), 115(2), 109, 352, 351(2), 351(3) of B haratiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (in short  ‘BNS’) and Section 27 of the Arms Act, is seeking for
being enlarged on regular bail on rejection by the Trial Court and the High
Court.
1

## Page 235

3. Having heard the learned Advocates appearing for the parties and on
perusal of the counter affidavit filed by the respondent it emerges from the
records that allegation made in the complaint is to the effect that appellant
and co-accused had arrived at the informant’s house with firearms and
lathis and  appellant had fired at the informant namely Binod Kumar
causing a gunshot injury in left thigh. 
4. The learned counsel appearing for the Appellant would contend that the
said FIR is a counter blast after they attacked the informant side and in
this regard, an FIR has also been registered in FIR No.298 of 2025 by the
appellant’s family alleging that informant side had attacked them with
sticks and Binod Kumar had fired from country made pistol 6 to 7 times.
Hence, Appellant seeks for grant of regular bail.
5. Having heard the learned Advocates appearing for the parties, it would
emerge from the records that co-accused have already been enlarged on
2

## Page 236

bail. Though there is a specific allegation of firing against the appellant,
the fact remains that, as per the averments made in the complaint that
other co-accused also had carried the firearms and they have been released
in bail. Even according to the prosecution there is no recovery of weapon
from the appellant. Hence, we are of the considered view that Appellant is
entitled for being released on regular bail. The Appeal is allowed and the
Impugned Order is hereby set aside and  Appellant is ordered to be
released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit and
appropriate by the jurisdictional Court.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (C) NO. 9018 OF 2026)
THE GENERAL MANAGER (HRD) & ANR.         ...APPELLANTS
VERSUS
NALAGANGU MOHAN SAI KRISHNA            ...RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties.
3. The respondent submitted his resignation vide  notice
dated 03.06.2025. Under Clauses (2) and (3) of Regulation
20 of the Punjab & Sind Bank (Officers’) Service Regulation,
1982 (for short, ‘the Service Regulations, 1982’), the
period of notice required for a resignation notice is three
months,  which  is  to  be  submitted  to  the  competent
authority; though the competent authority has the power to
reduce the period of notice or to remit the requirement of
notice.   However,  where  disciplinary  proceedings  are
pending against an officer, the notice is not to take effect
unless it is accepted by the competent authority.
4. As there were no disciplinary proceedings pending
1

## Page 243

against the respondent, on expiry of three months, the
resignation notice became effective.  However, instead of
accepting the resignation as effective, the appellant-Bank,
on 15.10.2025, initiated disciplinary proceedings against
the respondent. 
5. In  between,  as  the  Bank  had  not  relieved  the
respondent  from  service,  the  respondent  filed  a  writ
petition being W.P. No.24910 of 2025 before the High Court
of Andhra Pradesh at Amravati for issuance of a direction
upon the Bank to relieve him from service. 
6. The Bank contested the writ petition by claiming that
since the resignation notice was not accepted and, before
acceptance of the resignation notice, on 15.10.2025 a
decision was taken to initiate disciplinary proceedings
against the writ petitioner, he cannot be relieved from
service.
7. The learned Single Judge of the High Court after
interpreting clauses (2) and (3) of Regulation 20 of the
Service Regulations, 1982, came to the conclusion that
since no disciplinary proceedings were initiated within
three months from the date of receipt of the resignation
notice, the resignation became effective on 01.09.2025 and
thereafter, there existed no master-servant relationship to
enable the Bank to initiate disciplinary proceedings.
2

## Page 244

8. Consequently, the learned Single Judge allowed the
writ petition  vide  order dated 17.12.2025 and issued a
direction  to  the  Bank  to  issue  requisite  documents
relieving the respondent to enable him to join another
service/Bank.
9. Aggrieved by the order of the learned Single Judge,
the appellant-Bank filed an intra-Court appeal before the
Division Bench of the High Court.  The Division Bench,
though agreed with the view taken by the learned Single
Judge, in paragraphs 13 and 14 of the impugned order,
observed as under: 
“13. In view of the above and to protect
the interest of the respondent-Bank, it is
appropriate to direct the petitioner to
submit an undertaking to the respondent-
Bank stating that after completion of the
enquiry, if it is found that there is any
financial loss to the Bank, it would be
compensated  by  the  petitioner.  If  any
misappropriation or any charges requires
prosecution proceedings, it is always open
to the respondent-Bank to take steps in
accordance  with  law.  But  keeping  the
resignation  tendered  by  the  petitioner
pending without relieving him to join in
the State Bank of India is undoubtedly not
reasonable  and  justifiable.  For  the
aforesaid reasons, in our considered view,
there are no merits in the appeal either in
law or on facts and accordingly appeal
fails.
14. For the reasons stated above, the writ
appeal is disposed of with a direction to
the writ petitioner/respondent herein to
submit an undertaking to the respondent-
Bank stating that he would compensate any
3

## Page 245

financial loss to the Bank after completion
of the enquiry. It is made clear that the
Bank shall pay salary to the petitioner as
long as he continues, the service in the
respondent-Bank. There shall be no order as
to costs.”
10. The appellant-Bank has appealed against the said order
on the ground that if the master-servant relationship does
not survive after resignation had come into effect, there
was  no  occasion  to  continue  with  the  disciplinary
proceedings and therefore, the order passed by the Division
Bench needs to be modified.
11. We are of the view that although the observations in
paragraphs 13 and 14 of the impugned order, prima  facie,
are to protect the interest of the Bank, but, in law, if
the resignation had come into effect, the disciplinary
proceedings cannot be undertaken as there would be no
subsisting  master-servant  relationship  between  the
appellant-Bank and the respondent.  
12. In this context, the learned counsel appearing for the
appellants, submitted that the impugned order passed by the
Division Bench creates an anomalous situation inasmuch as,
on one hand, it accepts the order of the learned Single
Judge that the resignation has come into effect and on the
other, it directs the Bank to pay salary to the respondent
as long as he continues in service.
4

## Page 246

13. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellants
therefore submitted that he would have no objection if the
order passed by the Division Bench is modified to declare
that the services of the respondent/writ petitioner stood
terminated with effect from 01.09.2025 i.e., on the date
when his resignation came to be effective. However, the
respondent should not stake a claim to any salary after
01.09.2025.
14. The learned counsel for the respondent submits that he
would have no claim for salary if the order of the learned
Single Judge is restored.  
15. Having regard to the above submissions including the
provisions of Regulations 20(2) and 20(3) of the Service
Regulations, 1982, we are of the view that the order passed
by the learned Single Judge of the High Court was correct
and there was no necessity for the Division Bench to modify
the said order. Besides, once the resignation had come into
effect  on  01.09.2025,  there  was  no  master-servant
relationship surviving between the Bank and the respondent,
therefore, in absence of any rule or regulation permitting
disciplinary action after termination of master-servant
relationship, there was no occasion for the High Court to
permit the Bank to continue with the inquiry and subject
the respondent-writ petitioner to undertake that if in the
5

## Page 247

inquiry, the Bank finds any loss to have been caused by the
writ petitioner, the writ petitioner would recompense the
Bank.
16. In view of the above, we deem it appropriate to set
aside the impugned order passed by the Division Bench of
the High Court and restore the order passed by the learned
Single Judge in W.P. No. 24910 of 2025. 
17. Consequently, the undertaking, if any, filed by the
respondent pursuant to the impugned order of the Division
Bench, shall stand discharged.  Since we have affirmed and
restored  the  order  of  the  learned  Single  Judge,  the
appellant-Bank shall ensure that the relieving order is
issued to the respondent within a period of two weeks from
today.
18. The appeal stands disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
19. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.
………………………………………J.
  (MANOJ MISRA)
………………………………………J.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No. 253210/2026 - VACATING STAY
1. In this matter on 20 th August, 2026, this Court
passed the following order:
“1. Application  for  exemption  from  filing
certified  copy  of  the  impugned  judgment  is
allowed.
2. Heard  Mr.  Neeraj  Kishan  Kaul,  learned
senior counsel appearing for the petitioner.
3. Learned senior counsel contends that the
petitioner-hotel  has  subscribed  to  the  cable
operator who has a licence from the respondent-
Society.   Learned  senior  counsel  drawing
attention to paragraphs 28 and 40 of the judgment
of this Court in the case of Hotel & Restaurant
Assn & Another v. Star India (P) Ltd. & Others 1
contends that the petitioner is not transmitting
signals to any other person. On the contrary, the
petitioner is recipient of it.
4. Learned  senior  counsel  further  drawing
attention to Section 52(1)(k) of the Copyright
Act, 1957 submits that the said sub-clause only
deals with an ‘enclosed room meant for common
use’ and cannot be extended to individual rooms
in a hotel which obviously are not for common use
purposes.
5. Learned senior counsel also distinguishes
the judgment of the learned Single Judge of the
1 . (2006) 13 SCC 753
2

## Page 280

Delhi High Court in the case of Super Cassettes
Industries Ltd. v. Nirula Corner House (P) Ltd. 2
inter alia on the ground that not only was the
said judgment rendered in the context of an Order
VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
application but the said judgment did not notice
the judgment of this Court in Star India (supra).
6.  Learned senior counsel submits that the
Trial Court had rightly declined the injunction
and pending appeal, the respondent did not have
any  interim  order.   Learned  senior  counsel
submits that under the circumstances, to force
the  petitioner  to  seek  a  licence  from  the
respondent would be contrary to law.
 7. Issue notice, returnable on 12 th October,
2026.
8. Till the next date of hearing, there shall
be an interim stay of operation of the impugned
order.”

licences  and  authorisations,  including  the
requisite  copyright  licence  covering  the
television content services bring provided.
5

## Page 283

Accordingly, there is no legal or licensing
impediment to the operation of CCN television
services at Hotel Appolo, and the services may be
continued through our network in accordance with
the applicable licences and regulations.
Yours faithfully,
sd/-
        CCN Unit No.:-57/D”
11. The  letter  though  states  that  all  licences
including the requisite copyright licence are available,
it  does  not  say  that  there  is  a  licence  from  the
respondent-society.
12. We direct the petitioner to place the licence that
the cable operator possesses on record before the Court
on the next date of hearing.
13. List the application along with the main petition
on 9th September, 2026.

(Listing) for appropriate action.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.3937/2026)
TECHI KAK ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
KAPWANG LETEY LOWANG & ORS. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant-informant;
learned counsel for the State of Arunachal Pradesh- Respondent
No.2; and learned counsel for respondent Nos. 1 and 3.
3. In this case, notice was issued way back on 25.02.2026.
However no counter affidavit has been filed on behalf of the
respondent  No.2,  though  respondent  No.1  has  filed  counter
affidavit. Therefore, we proceed to hear the matter on the basis of
available materials on record.
4. Appellant-informant is aggrieved by grant of bail by the
Guwahati High Court, Itanagar Bench, (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter) to the first respondent.
1

## Page 285

5. Assailing the order of the High Court, learned counsel for the
appellant submits that the High Court has only gone by the
principle of parity considering that co-accused Lishi Roni was
granted bail by this Court. High Court did not independently
examine any other relevant factors while considering the bail
application of the first respondent. In this connection, he has
referred  to  the  materials  on  record  including  the  statement
recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973,
(CrPC). He submits that parity cannot be the sole consideration for
grant of bail. In support of such a contention, he has placed
reliance on a decision of this Court in Sagar vs. State of Uttar
Pradesh, 2025 SCC onLine SC 2584. He further submits that insofar
antecedents are concerned, respondent No.1 has a number of criminal
antecedents  which  were  over-looked  by  the  High  Court.  While
considering the prayer for bail, antecedents as well as the
statements recorded under Section 161 CrPC are required to be
considered. Since these were not considered by the High Court,
therefore, the impugned order dated 13.11.2025, passed by the High
Court is liable to be set aside.
6. Learned counsel for respondent No.2 submits that out of the
total 43 witnesses, 22 witnesses were examined. However, as per
order of this Court, 6 of them have been directed to be recalled
and their deposition taken afresh. Now a date has been fixed for
the deposition of these witnesses.
6.1. On a query by the Court, she submits that state has not filed
2

## Page 286

any Special Leave Petition assailing the order of bail granted in
favour of the first respondent.
7. Learned counsel for the first respondent submits that there is
no reason why the order granting bail needs to be interfered with.
The  High  Court  has  considered  various  factors  including  the
principle of parity while granting bail to the first respondent.
All allegations made by the appellant qua the first respondent are
not  correct  and  nothing  has  been  recovered  from  the  first
respondent. Therefore, the appeal may be dismissed.
8. We have given our anxious consideration to the submissions
made at the Bar.
9. While there is no dispute to the proposition that parity
cannot be the sole ground for enlarging the accused on bail, the
fact, however, remains that it is certainly one of the relevant
considerations while examining the plea for bail. That apart,
insofar antecedents and consideration of statements made under
Section 161 CrPC is concerned, certainly these are also factors
which need to be considered by the court while examining bail. But
in a case relating to bail it will all depend on the facts and
circumstances of each case. No hard and fast rule can be laid down
for a court to decide in which way and in what manner a bail
application is required to be considered.
10. On going through the impugned order of the High Court and
3

## Page 287

other materials on record, we find that the first respondent was
arrested on 13.11.2020. After conclusion of the investigation, the
charge-sheet was filed whereafter trial in Sessions Case No.2 of
2021 has commenced. It has been 5 years since then. Out of the 43
witnesses  cited  by  the  prosecution,  22  witnesses  have  been
examined. But 6 out of these 22 witnesses have been directed to be
recalled by this Court. Therefore, as of today, practically there
are 27 witnesses to be examined. On the date when the High Court
considered the bail application of the first respondent, he was
already in jail for 5 years. The length of detention of an under-
trial is certainly one of the most important considerations while
examining bail. It cannot be the proposition that while the trial
is unending with huge number of witnesses, the under-trial would
continue to remain incarcerated. This is certainly not the law of
the land. In paragraph 7 of the impugned order, we find that the
High Court has considered the length of detention, the progress of
the trial and the aspect of parity while granting bail to the first
respondent. Therefore, it cannot be said that the High Court
granted bail to the first respondent solely by applying the
principle of parity.
11. The impugned order granting bail was passed on 13.11.2025.
Today is 01.09.2026. More than 10 months have passed since the
first respondent was granted bail. Considering the above, we are
not inclined to interfere with the order granting bail. Therefore,
the prayer made for cancellation of bail stands rejected.
4

## Page 288

12. However, having regard to the nature of the allegations qua
the first respondent, we direct that till the conclusion of the
trial, he shall appear before the concerned police station i.e.,
Banderdewa Police Station on the first Monday of every month at
11:00 am to record his presence and to assure the authorities that
he is not or he will not indulge in any illegal activity. It goes
without saying that the first respondent shall cooperate with the
ongoing trial without fail till conclusion of the trial.
[
13. Subject to the above observations, the appeal is disposed of.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
......................J.
(UJJAL BHUYAN)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       /2026
  [@ SLP [CRL.] NO.11731/2026]
 
ASFAQ                               Appellant(s)
                      VERSUS
THE STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS.   Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
The appellant stands convicted under Section
3(2)(i) of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities
(Prevention) Act, 1987 (hereinafter referred to as
‘TADA’)  read with Section 120B of the Indian
Penal  Code,  1860  (hereinafter  referred  to  as
‘IPC’), Section 3(2)(ii), 3(3), 5, 6(1) of the

## Page 309

2
TADA, Section 302 read with Section 120B, 307,
326, 324, 436 of the IPC, Sections 3, 4 of the
Explosive Substances Act, 1908, Section 9-B, of
Explosive Act, 1884, Sections 150-151 of Railways
Act, 1989, Section 4 of Prevention of Damage to
Public Property Act, 1984.  He has been sentenced
to undergo imprisonment for life. His application
for emergent parole on account of illness of his
wife was rejected by the High Court.  Aggrieved,
he is before us.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties. The present appeal is against the
rejection of emergent parole on the premise that
the sons of the appellant can very well take care
of his wife.
After hearing the learned counsel appearing
for the parties, there is no dispute on the
ailment that is being suffered by the wife of the
appellant. She is suffering from stage IV colon
cancer.

## Page 310

3
The availability of the sons per se cannot be
a ground to deny the emergent parole. In fact, on
an earlier occasion on 25.07.2025, parole was
granted on the very same ground by the authority
and the appellant had complied with the terms and
conditions imposed thereunder.
We are inclined to take note of the earlier
orders passed by this Court in MA No.1178/2018 in
Civil Appeal No.10464/2017 dated 14.05.2018. 
Therefore, we are inclined to dispose of the
present  appeal  on  the  aforesaid  premise  by
granting emergent parole for a period of two weeks
from the date of his release on the same terms.
Accordingly, the appellant shall be released
on parole for a period of two weeks from the date
of his release.  However, we direct that, during
the aforesaid period, he shall report to the
Station House Officer of the concerned Police
Station on every third day.
The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly.

have been relied upon or used against the party in
whose absence it was prepared.

back to the Tehsildar to decide the issue in question
afresh in accordance with law, without being influenced

R4 RAFEEK AHAMED
