O R D E R
Heard Mr. M.Sathyanarayanan, learned Senior counsel
for the petitioner and Ms. Pariksha, learned Counsel for
the respondent no.1. 
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of an order dated
18.06.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Madras, Madurai Bench in CRP(NPD)(MD) No.1521 of 2021, by
which, the petition filed by the respondent no.1 herein
to permit her to satisfy the decree by paying the amount
involved has been allowed, upturning the rejection of the
same by the Execution Court/Trial Court.
1

## Page 337

4. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellant submitted
that pursuant to a money decree in his favour, during
execution, the property in question was sold in Court
auction and the same was purchased by respondents no.4
and 5 and they were put in possession thereof. It was
contended that the respondent no.1 after a delay of 875
days had filed an appeal against the judgment and decree
in favour of the appellant passed by the Trial Court in
the original suit. The same was rejected as the delay in
filing of the appeal was not condoned by the First
Appellate Court. However, the High Court has condoned the
delay under the order impugned. 
5. It was submitted that by reviving the proceedings
once again, the High Court under the order impugned, had
not only set the clock back, but has prejudiced the
rights that had crystallized. It was contended that in
the facts and circumstances of the case, the delay was
not fit to be condoned in any way for the reason that the
respondent no.1 had appeared in the Suit and was examined
as DW-3. Thus, it was contended that such delay does not
stand to reason and ought not to have been condoned.
6. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1 submitted
that no prejudice is going to be caused to the parties as
basically the appellant wanted his money, which she is
ready  to  pay.  It  was  further  contended  that  the
2

## Page 338

respondents no.4 and 5 have not objected to the impugned
order and thus, the same needs no interference. However,
with regard to the stand taken by learned Senior Counsel
for  the  appellant  with  regard  to  there  being  no
justification  for  delay,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent no.1 was not able to satisfy this Court as to
why such delay deserves to be condoned.
7. Having considered the matter in its entirety, we
find that the order impugned cannot be sustained, as the
decree  has  attained  finality  and  execution  stood
completed. Just because the respondent no.1 is ready to
pay the auction price, would not constitute sufficient
cause for condoning the huge delay. Even otherwise, we
find that once legal measures are taken by the parties
and the matter has attained finality, it is in the
fitness of things that the position is not changed on
flimsy grounds, that too, when it would lead to grave
consequences, both in law as also in real terms in view
of the time it will take for such proceedings to finally
conclude.
8. For the reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed.
The order impugned stands set aside and the appeal filed
by the respondent no.1 before the Principal District
Court, Theni, stands dismissed.
9. It goes without saying that any steps taken/money
3

## Page 339

deposited by the respondent no.1 pursuant to the order
impugned, would be returned to the respondent no.1 in
accordance with law.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the appellant.
3. Having regard to the nature of the order that we propose
to pass, we do not deem it necessary to issue notice to
the respondents.
4. The appellant is aggrieved by an order of the Rajasthan
High Court dated 02.07.2026 passed in writ petition
(i.e., DBCWP No. 16856/2019) whereby, on ground of
failure to remove certain encroachments, the appellant
amongst others have been directed to be placed under
suspension  till  conclusion  of  disciplinary  inquiry
against them.
1

## Page 342

5. As the impugned direction is found in an interim order
which has been passed for non-compliance of directions
of the High Court to remove encroachments, we decline to
interfere with the order insofar as it directs holding a
disciplinary inquiry. 
6. However, the direction to the Revenue Secretary to place
those  officers  under  suspension  till  departmental
proceedings are concluded is not justified because the
culpability of those officers would have to be examined
and determined by the disciplinary authority based on
materials available against them.   
7. In our view, the High Court ought to have left it for
the disciplinary authority to take such appropriate
action against them as it may be considered necessary,
particularly, when those officers/ employees are yet to
be either charged or punished for contempt of High
Court’s order. We, therefore, deem it appropriate to
expunge paragraph 5 in the impugned order whereby the
officers/ employees concerned have been directed to be
placed  under  suspension  pending  conclusion  of
disciplinary enquiry.
 
8. Consequently, this appeal is disposed of by expunging
2

## Page 343

that part of the direction as is found in paragraph 5 of
the impugned order dated 02.07.2026.
9. However, we make it clear that if the disciplinary
authority is of the opinion that any of those persons
are negligent in performance of their duties, it shall
be open for the disciplinary authority to take such
appropriate action against them, including suspension
pending inquiry, as it may deem appropriate on the basis
of their conduct.
10. In  case  the  appellant  has  already  been  suspended
pursuant to the direction in paragraph 5 of the impugned
order, the disciplinary authority shall review the order
of suspension and if in its opinion no material is found
against him, it may recall the same subject to final
orders in the proceedings pending before the High Court.
 
11. The appeal as well as all pending applications shall
stand disposed of in the aforesaid terms.

      Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We heard the learned senior counsel appearing for the
petitioner and the learned senior counsel appearing for
the State,  the Co-Operative  Housing Society  and the
Intervenors who are the beneficiaries.
2

## Page 358

SLP(C)  No.  9037/2024
2. The subject matter of the Public Interest Litigation
before the High Court was with respect to grant of lands
to government employees who formed themselves into a Co-
operative Society. By the order dated 07.04.2026, we had
directed the State to file a report as to the specific
questions raised by us in the said order. Today the
Secretary  to  Government,  Revenue  Departments  (Land
Revenue), has filed an affidavit dated 29.07.2026.
3. The subject allotment is with respect to two separate
parcels of government land, one having an extent of 55
acres and the other having an extent of 100 acres.
Insofar as the 55 acres land, the developed layout has
845 plots, out of which 743 plots have constructed houses
and 11 are remaining with compound walls, with 91 plots
remaining vacant. Insofar as the land of 100 acres is
concerned,  1615  plots  have  been  earmarked  in  the
partially developed layout, out of which, 6 plots have
permanent residential structures, 3 plots have semi-
constructed structures and 18 have temporary rooms. The
remaining 1588 plots are vacant due to the pending case. 
4. As  far  as  the  eligibility  is  concerned,  the
3

## Page 359

SLP(C)  No.  9037/2024
compliance affidavit indicates that any employee who has
put in minimum of 5 years of service, is eligible,
provided he does not have a house in Hyderabad or Ranga
Reddy Districts. It is clarified that if both the spouses
are  employed,  then  only  one  would  be  entitled  to
allotment. It has also been stated on instructions that
the two parcels of land are far from the Secretariat and
they are intended as retirement homes, especially to the
marginalized section of employees working in the lower
cadres of government service. 
5. However,  we  do  not  see  such  an  eligibility
restriction insofar as only the lower grade employees
being made eligible to apply under the notification. We
were  also told  that there  is a  restriction on  the
transfer of the land within a period of 10 years.
6. In this context, what troubled us was the eligibility
requirement of a person to have only 5 years of service
in the State so as to apply for allotment. Hence, a
person  who had  a service  period of  5 years,  could
transfer the allotted plot within another 10 years even
while he is in service, which does not necessarily enable
4

## Page 360

SLP(C)  No.  9037/2024
him  to  have  a  roof  over  his  head  at  the  time  of
retirement. We also do not find any restriction insofar
as lease of the houses constructed therein.
7. On the above apprehensions expressed, we are of the
opinion that Government should file a report specifically
indicating the persons allotted, their designation, their
period  of  service  and  specifying  those  who  had
constructed  lands  and  the  others,  whose  lands  are
remaining  vacant.  The  table  should  be  prepared
categorizing persons having 5-10 years’ service, 10-20
years’ service and so on, putting together persons having
service in a 10 year period and also indicating the age
of even person allotted plots in the two parcels of land.
 
8. The affidavit shall be filed within a period of six
weeks from today.
9. List on 28.10.2026.

THE STATE OF HARYANA & ORS. RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. We have heard Mr. Rameshwar Singh Malik, learned senior
counsel for the appellant, Mr. Nikhil Goel, learned Additional
1

## Page 367

Advocate General for the State of Haryana and learned counsel
appearing for the private respondents.
2. The writ petition of the appellant was allowed by a Single
Judge of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh by an
order dated 13th June, 2016 by applying the principle “old vacancy,
old rule” in a promotion related dispute. Inspiration was drawn from
the decision of this Court in Y.V.Rangaiah Vs. J. Sreenivasa Rao1
which, indeed, laid down the rule that vacancies arising prior to
amendment of promotion rules ought to be filled up in accordance
with the rules then existing when the vacancies occurred.
3. However, the Division Bench of the High Court in appeal
against the order of the Single Judge noted that the principle of law
laid down in Y. V. Rangaiah (supra) had been doubted in a number
of subsequent decisions although there was no express overruling of
such decision.
4. The final nail in the coffin of the rule of “old vacancy, old rule”
laid down in Y. V. Rangaiah (supra) is driven by the 3-Judge Bench
decision of this Court in State of Himachal Pradesh Vs. Raj
Kumar2 where  Y. V. Rangaiah  (supra) has been expressly
overruled. The decision in Raj Kumar (supra) has recently been
followed by a coordinate Bench of this Court in State of Orissa Vs.
Sreepati Ranjan Dash3.
5. Having regard to the principles laid down in  Raj Kumar
1  (1983) 3 SCC 284
2  (2023) 3 SCC 773
3  2026 INSC 505
2

## Page 368

(supra) and  Sreepati Ranjan Dash  (supra), we are of the
considered opinion that the order of the Division Bench under
challenge requiring aspirants for promotion to be graduates, in
terms of the amended rules, does not warrant any interference. 
6. The civil appeals are, accordingly, dismissed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Jaideep Gupta and Mr. Raghenth Basant,
learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioners, Mr.
Shyam Divan, Ms. Liz Mathew and Mr. Anirban Ray, learned
senior  counsel  appearing  on  caveat  on  behalf  of
respondent No.1.
2. Delay condoned.
3. The  present  petitions  call  in  question  the
correctness of the judgment dated 31 st March, 2026 passed
by the Division Bench of the High Court at Calcutta in
FMA No. 250 of 2026 and FMA No.64 of 2026.
4. The facts of the case, briefly stated, are as
follows:
The first respondent filed Title Suit No.120 of
2026 before the 2 nd Civil Judge (Senior Division) at
Alipore for certain declaratory and injunctory reliefs.
Along with the Suit, an application under Order XXXIX
Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (for
short, “CPC”)  was filed praying for ex-parte ad-interim
injunction  restraining  the  petitioners  herein,  inter
alia, from dealing with the suit scheduled A1 properties
from creating any third party rights, pursuant to the
settlement dated 13 th March, 2019.  The Trial Court, on
2

## Page 409

28th January,  2026  granted  the  ex-parte  ad-interim
injunction.  
5. This  order  was  carried  in  the  appeal  by  the
petitioners herein resulting in the impugned order.  The
impugned order has confirmed the ex-parte ad-interim
order. Though multifarious reasons have been given in the
impugned order and in fact a question of law has also
been referred to a larger Bench, we are not inclined to
discuss the same, considering the nature of the order
that we propose to make.  
6. Undisputedly, the order dated 28 th January, 2026
passed by the Trial Court was an ex-parte ad-interim
order.  It is not disputed that the petitioner-Akshay
Vinimay LLP in SLP (Civil) Diary No.42819 of 2026 has in
fact already invoked its remedies under Order XXXIX Rule
4 of the CPC before the Trial Court.
7. The remedy under Order XXXIX Rule 4 of the CPC
having been availed, it is only fit and proper that the
said application is decided after both parties are heard.
8. At this stage,  learned senior counsel appearing
for the petitioners expressed an apprehension that the
observations made in the impugned order will come in the
way of the disposal of the Order XXXIX Rule 4 of the CPC
application and will operate to their prejudice.
3

## Page 410

9. We make it clear that the Order XXXIX Rule 4 remedy
which the petitioners have availed/may avail will be
decided independently on its own merits, uninfluenced by
any of the observations either in the order of the High
Court or in the present order that we have now made.  We
also direct that considering the nature of the dispute,
the Order XXXIX Rule 4 application should be decided
within eight weeks from today by the Trial Court.
10. With  the  above  observations,  the  Special  Leave
Petitions are disposed of.
11. Pending applications shall stand disposed of.
(ANITA MALHOTRA)                       (JAYANT RAJ KATYAL)

dismissed the appellants’ appeal which, in turn, was
preferred against the order dated 17.02.2023 passed by
the Railway Claims Tribunal, Principal Bench (for short,
‘the Tribunal’) in OA/II(U)/DLI/131/2022.
3. The Tribunal, in turn, rejected appellants’
claim seeking compensation on account of death of their
son, Kapil Goel.
4. Upon hearing learned counsel for the parties
and keeping in view the ends of justice, we are of the
considered  view  that  the  High  Court  should  have
entertained the appeal on merits after condoning the
delay.
5. Accordingly,  the  appeal  is  allowed.  The
impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside and
delay in filing the appeal before the High Court is
condoned.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.13726/2026)
SANJAY KUMAR @ CHAPAN ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Ajay Marwah, learned counsel for the
appellant  and  Ms.  Sanya  Kaushal,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent- State of Himachal Pradesh.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 09.01.2026, passed by
the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter) passed in Criminal MP (M) No.2734 of 2025, rejecting
the bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in FIR No.62 of 2025,
registered at Dharamshala Police Station, District- Kangra, in the
State of Himachal Pradesh, under Section 20 of the Narcotic Drugs
and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS Act’).
5. Case  of  the  prosecution  is  that  acting  on  a  secret
information, police searched the residence of the appellant in the
1

## Page 436

intervening night of 06.04.2025. At that stage, appellant and co-
accused Suman Kumari were found on the first floor of the premises.
They were brought down by the police to the ground floor from where
1.26 kgs of Cannabis were recovered, following which appellant and
co-accused Suman Kumari were arrested in the night of 06.04.2025
itself.
6. This Court by order dated 24.07.2026 had issued notice.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that it is a matter
of record that the house where the search was carried out has 5
owners including the appellant. Therefore, the entire blame, if
any, cannot be fastened on to the appellant. That apart, the laid
down procedure for conducting such raid after sunset or before
sunrise has not been followed. He also makes a submission regarding
the sampling of the seized contraband and examination of the same
by the forensic laboratory.
8. On the other hand, learned State counsel has referred to the
averments made in the counter affidavit and submits that the
contentions of the appellant are a matter of trial. She submits
that trial is proceeding and as of today, 5 prosecution witnesses
have been examined though 14 still remain to be examined.
9. We have given our anxious consideration to the submissions
made at the Bar.
10. Appellant has now been in custody for more than 1 year 4
months. Whether the procedure has been followed while carrying out
the seizure of the contraband and examination thereof by the
forensic laboratory are all matters of trial. However, the fact
that the premises from where the seizure was made belongs to 5
2

## Page 437

owners is a factor which cannot be ignored even at the time of
consideration of bail of the appellant. That apart, with 14 more
witnesses still to be examined, early conclusion of the trial does
not appear to be a reasonable possibility.
11. In the circumstances, we are of the view that a case for grant
of bail is made out.
12. We accordingly set aside the impugned order of the High Court
dated 09.01.2026, passed by the High Court in Criminal MP (M)
No.2734 of 2025 and direct that the appellant shall be produced
before the jurisdictional Special Judge within a maximum period of
7 days from today whereafter he shall be released on bail on such
terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
13. Criminal Appeal is accordingly allowed.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Leave granted.
2. Admittedly, the writ petitions before the learned Single Judge
are  still  pending  for  adjudication  on  merits  regarding  the
alignment of the road, in which the decision of the Jaipur
Development Authority is under challenge. During the pendency of
the writ petitions before the learned Single Judge, directions were
issued as an interim measure to remove the constructions of the
appellants, which order was taken up in appeals before the Division
Bench. The Division Bench dismissed the appeals, resulting in the
filing of the present appeals.
3. In our considered view, once the writ petitions itself were
pending before the learned Single Judge for consideration on merits
regarding the alignment of the road in question, it was unjustified
of the learned Single Judge to have directed removal of the
constructions of the writ petitioners, i.e., the appellants herein.
The Division Bench also erred in dismissing the appeals.
1

## Page 444

4. In view of the above, we request the learned Single Judge to
decide the pending writ petitions on merits.
5. Till the disposal of the said writ petitions, the parties
shall maintain  status  quo  with regard to the constructions in
question.
6. Any observations made in the common impugned order shall not
influence the learned Single Judge in deciding the matter on its
merits in accordance with law.
7. With the above observations, the appeals stand disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

1. Delay condoned.

3. The appellant has been convicted by
the Trial Court i.e., Additional Sessions
Judge,  Deogarh  in  Sessions  Case  No.
S.T.16/2010 by order dated 08.10.2010 and
has been convicted for committing offence
under Section 302/34 of Indian Penal Code,
1860  and  was  sentenced  to  undergo  life
imprisonment.
4. Challenging  his  conviction  and
sentence,  appellant  preferred  Criminal
Appeal No.236 of 2016 before the High Court
of Orrisa along with an application under
Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to
condone the delay of 1974 days in filing the
appeal. The said application was registered
as  Misc.  Case  No.671  of  2016.  By  the
impugned order, the said application has

## Page 456

2
been rejected on the ground that there is no
explanation at all to condone the delay of
1974 days in filing the appeal.
5. In  a  recent  judgment  rendered  by
this Court in the case of  Arjun Jani @
Tuntun  versus  State  of  Orissa  (Criminal
Appeal No. 3639/2026 ), this Court has held
that  a  criminal  appeal  preferred  by  a
convict, who is in jail, should not be
dismissed  on  the  ground  of  delay  in
preferring the appeal.
6. In  the  present  case  also,  the
appellant is in jail for about 19 years.
Even in the year 2016, the appellant was in
jail for about 09 years and on the date of
consideration  by  the  High  Court,  the
appellant was in jail. Therefore, the High
Court should have taken a lenient view of
the matter and condoned the delay.
7. For the above stated reasons, the
impugned order passed by the High Court is
set aside; and the matter is remitted back
to the High Court for consideration the
appellant’s appeal on its own merits at an
early date. Appellant’s prayer before the
High Court for condoning the delay occurred
in filing the appeal in Misc. Case No. 671

before the High Court is restored to its

1. The  de  facto complainant  is  here  before  us  being
dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High
Court dated 08.10.2025 in two Criminal Appeal Nos.671/2017 and
688/2017, respectively, by which both the appeals came to be
partly allowed by affirming the judgment and order of conviction
of the respondents before us (original accused persons) by the
Trial Court, however, granting benefit of Section 4 of the
Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 (for short, “the Act, 1958”).
2. The operative part of the impugned order reads thus:-
“43. Taking note of above, the conviction of the
appellants  namely  Shiv  Kumar  and  Onkar  Nath  is
maintained for the offence under Section 308 I.P.C.,
as witnesses of facts including injured witnesses
Murari Lal (PW-2) and Shiv Sahai Singh, Pharmacist
(PW-4) established the case of prosecution before the
trial court, and sentence is modified. Instead of
sending  the  appellants  to  jail,  they  are  given
benefit of Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders
Act, 1958 and are directed to file two sureties each
to the tune of Rs 20,000/- along with personal bonds
before District Probation Officer concerned and also
2

## Page 469

SLP (Crl.)  Nos.6984-6985/2026
an undertaking to the effect they shall maintain
peace and good behaviour during the period of one
year from today. The said bonds are to be filed by
the appellants within a period of three months from
the date of this judgment. 
44.  The  accused-appellants  within  the  aforesaid
period shall also deposit the amount of fine before
the trial Court, as imposed in the judgment, under
appeal, if the same has not been deposited till date.
45. In case of breach of any of the above conditions,
the appellants shall be taken into custody and shall
have to undergo sentence awarded to them.”
3. It is the case of petitioner that High Court Committed an
egregious error in giving benefit of Section 4 of the Act, 1958
to the respondents-original accused persons.  The main bone of
contention is that the order is in  breach of sub-section (2) of
Section 4 of the Act, 1958, which according to the learned
counsel mandates the Court to call for the report of the
probation officer before giving benefit of probation to the
accused.
4. Prima facie, it appears from the materials on record that
no such report was called for.  All that weighed with the High
Court was the fact that incident had occurred almost 22 years
back and there were no criminal antecedents of the accused

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.441 OF 2018
STATE OF UTTARAKHAND                      Appellant(s)
VERSUS
RAJU                                     Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. This appeal by the State is against the judgment
and  order  of  the  High  Court1 dated  11.12.2014
passed in Criminal Appeal No.179 of 2010 whereby
the criminal appeal of the respondent was allowed,
and the judgment and order of the trial Court
convicting the respondent under Section 302/201
I.P.C. and Section 4/25 of the Arms Act was set
aside; and the respondent was acquitted of the
charges for which he was tried.
2. On 06.03.2006 at 8.30 AM a dead body was found in
an  open  field  with  cut  on  the  neck.  During
investigation, the body was identified to be one of
Sukra. The case set up against the respondent was
that he had been in an illicit relationship with
the deceased, and at 10:30 p.m. on 05.03.2006 he
11 The High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital 
1

## Page 472

was  noticed  in  the  company  of  the  deceased.
Besides, based on his disclosure statement, a knife
was recovered alleged to have been used in the
crime. 
3. Primarily on the aforesaid two circumstances, the
trial court convicted the respondent.
4. The High Court found, from the evidence on record,
that insofar as the evidence of last seen is
concerned, it was inconclusive inasmuch as even if
the evidence was accepted, the deceased and the
accused were seen together near Dak Bungalow at
night which was far away from the place where the
body of the deceased was found; therefore, as
there had been a huge time gap between the last
seen circumstance and the recovery of the body,
intervening circumstances including involvement of
a third person cannot be ruled out. As far as the
recovery of knife is concerned, admittedly, the
same was not forensically connected with the crime.
In such circumstances, the High Court deemed it
appropriate to set aside the order of conviction
and acquit the respondent.
5. We have considered the submissions of the learned
counsel for the parties. We do not find any error
in the view taken by the High Court. Besides, last
seen circumstance is a weak piece of evidence.
2

## Page 473

Ordinarily,  on  its  own,  a  conviction  is  not
sustainable unless and until there is very little
time gap between the last seen circumstance and
recovery of the dead body to rule out intervening
circumstances including involvement of any third
party in the crime. Here, the weapon allegedly
recovered has not been forensically connected to
the crime. We, therefore, find no good reason to
interfere with the order passed by the High Court.
6. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.
. . . . . . . . . . .,J
[MANOJ MISRA]      
. . . . . . . . . . .,J
[VIJAY BISHNOI]    
NEW DELHI;
SEPTEMBER 1st, 2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA     CORRECTED
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICATION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 10959 OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO. 15152 OF 2025    
MOHINDER SINGH           ...APPELLANT
VERSUS
BHAGWAN DASS AND ORS. ...RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the parties. 
3. Though  arguments  have  been  made  on  merits  with
respect to the scope and application of Rule 69 of the
Haryana  Panchayati  Raj  Election  Rules,  1994  and
interpretation of Section 176 of the Haryana Panchayati Raj
Act, 1994, we are inclined to set aside the impugned order
passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana only on the
premise that no reasons have been adduced by the high court
except reproducing the basis upon which the order impugned
before it was predicated. 
4. In such view of the matter, the impugned order passed
by the High Court is set aside and the matter is remitted
to the High Court for fresh consideration to decide all the
issues  both  on  law  and  facts.  All  the  issues  are,
1

## Page 480

accordingly, left open.  
5. We request the High Court to make an endeavour to
expeditiously dispose of the matter preferably within a
period of three months from the date of receipt of a copy
of this order, particularly, by taking note of the fact
that we are dealing with an election petition for which,
time is a relevant factor.
6. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

government service. They retired a long time ago, and some of them
have now unfortunately passed away. The applicants seek permission
in terms of the order dated 02.11.2012 passed by this Court, to
sell the said plots allotted to them or their predecessors.

permission is granted to them to sell the allotted plots, subject

Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C)  No.30618/2026:-
1. We heard Mr. Shyam Divan, the learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the petitioner, Mr. Navin Pahwa, the learned
Senior counsel appearing for the Respondent Nos.1 and 2
respectively, Mr. Gaurav Agarwal, the learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the Respondent No.3 - Bank and Mr. Vinay Garg,
the learned Counsel appearing for the borrowers.
2. The subject - matter of challenge in the present petition
is the Order passed by the High Court dated 29th July, 2026 in
Writ Petition No.30195/2026 preferred by the Respondent Nos.1
and  2  respectively  before  us,  by  which  the  High  Court
dismissed the writ petition in the following terms:-
“9. By way of this petition, the petitioners are assailing the
order  passed  by  21.07.2026  (Annexure  P-27)  passed  by  DRAT,
Allahabad, and DRT and order dated 30.06.2026 (Annexure P-25)
passed by the District Magistrate Bhopal under section 14 of the
SARFAESI Act inter alia on the ground that civil suit (counter
claim) is still pending challenging the gift deed in favour of
the borrower i.e Smt. Mallika Garg; therefore, the DRT and DRAT,
Allahabad have wrongly dismissed the S.A and appeal on the ground

## Page 493

3
of locus. It is also submitted that the District Magistrate has
wrongly passed the order for taking physical possession during
pendency of the suit.
10. So far the civil suit is concerned, the application under
Order 39 Rule 2 of C.P.C filed by the petitioner had already been
dismissed long back. The District Magistrate earlier dismissed,
the application under section 14, which became the subject matter
of W.P no. 14869/2018. The sole ground of the petitioner had been
rejected in paragraph 7, i.e respondent nos. 5 to 7 therein i.e.,
the present petitioner succeeded in the counterclaim. They might
have a claim against Smt. Mallika Garg, not against the Bank. The
aforesaid order has been upheld by the Apex Court by dismissing
the  SLP.  Therefore,  now  the  petitioner  cannot  question  the
proceeding initiated under the SARFAESI Act by the Bank under
section 13 and 14 of the SARPAESI Act and cannot resist the
physical possession to be taken by the respondent/Bank. Hence,
the petition is dismissed.
11. However, the petitioners shall have a liberty to clear the
debt amount in total if they want to protect the mortgaged House
No. E-2/8, Arera Colony, Bhopal (M.P) from auction. If the
petitioners have bona fide intentions and submit a proposal for
full and final settlement of the Loan Account within one month
from today with a Demand Draft of Rs. One Crores, the Respondent
No.l/ Bank shall consider it before finalising the auction
proceedings in accordance with the SARFAESI Act.”

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. This Special Leave Petition is directed against the judgment
dated 07.08.2025 whereby the High Court while dismissing the
second appeal recorded a finding that respondent is the owner
1 of 3

## Page 511

of the suit property by virtue of registered sale deed and
granted liberty to him to take recourse to remedy available to
secure possession separately.
3. Facts giving rise to filing of this petition in a nutshell are
that respondent filed a suit seeking recovery of possession of
the suit property, arrears of rent, and mesne profits. The
trial court by a judgment and decree dated 16.12.1988 granted
arrears of rent for a limited period but refused the relief of
possession. The suit was partly decreed. Being aggrieved, the
petitioner preferred an appeal. The First Appellate Court vide
judgment and decree dated 01.01.1993 allowed the appeal and
dismissed the suit in its entirety. The High Court vide
impugned judgment and decree dated 07.08.2025 dismissed the
second appeal but held that respondent is the owner of the suit
property and is entitled to take recourse to remedy available
to secure possession separately. 
4. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  parties,  Mr.
Shashibhushan P. Adgaonkar, learned counsel for petitioner is
correct in his submission that the High Court could not have
made observations with regard to ownership and title of the
respondent/plaintiff for the reason that the suit was only for
arrears of rent and possession. 
5. In this view of the matter, we clarify that observation made by
the High Court in the impugned judgment shall not have any
bearing on any subsequent suit(s)/proceedings pending between
the parties and the suit(s) shall be decided on its own merits.
6. With the aforesaid clarification, the Special Leave Petition is
2 of 3

## Page 512

disposed of.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

inclined to suspend the sentence of the petitioner and
enlarge her on bail, pending hearing of the Criminal

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
 (arising out of SLP(C) No. 23958/2023)
VRINDAVAN CHATURVEDI APPELLANT(S)
                         VERSUS
PUSHPA DEVI KHEMKA & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. We find that the Division Bench of the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh, Principal Seat at Jabalpur, non-suited the appellant,
Vrindavan Chaturvedi, in his writ appeal on the ground that
though the writ petition filed by the respondents was under
Article 226 of the Constitution of India, it should be treated
as one filed under Article 227 of the Constitution of India
and against such an order, an appeal would not lie.
3. Reliance is sought to be placed by the learned counsel
appearing for the respondents to support this view of the High
Court by citing the earlier Division Bench judgment of the
Madhya Pradesh High Court in Dangalia  vs.  Deshraj1. However,
we note from the said judgment that the Division Bench
specifically noted therein that reversal of orders passed by
the Revenue Courts could as well be in writ proceedings under
Article 226 of the Constitution of India apart from Article
1(1977) MP series 739
1

## Page 559

227. 
4. It is well settled that the extraordinary jurisdiction and
powers  of  the  High  Courts  under  Article  226  of  the
Constitution of India cannot be scuttled or whittled down by
any legislation. 
5. Further, Revenue Courts that exercise statutory quasi-judicial
powers cannot be equated to or be treated on par with judicial
Courts. Validity of orders passed by such Revenue Courts can
be tested before the High Court under its writ jurisdiction.
6. In that view of the matter, the understanding of the Division
Bench that though the respondents filed a writ petition under
Article 226 of the Constitution of India, it should be treated
as one filed under Article 227, so as to deny the appellant
the appellate remedy of an appeal, cannot be sustained. 
7. The impugned order dated 20.07.2023 is set aside and Writ
Appeal No. 576/2023 is restored to the file of the High Court
to be considered afresh on its own merits and in accordance
with law. All issues are left open. 
8. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed in the aforestated terms.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
......................J.
(SANJAY KUMAR)
......................J.

1. HON’BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN pronounced the judgment
of the Bench comprising HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA a nd His
Lordship.
2. The appeals are allowed in terms of the signed non reportable
judgment.
3. The relevant part of the signed non reportable judgment is as
under:-
“11. We  are  unable  to  find  the
prosecution  having  established  the
culpability  of  the  accused  beyond
reasonable doubt. As we noticed, the eye-
witness  testimony  does  not  inspire
confidence and there are no recoveries
made or seizures effected as would have
been done in a proper investigation. The
case is not of a faulty investigation but
of no investigation having been carried
out. Even the inquest was carried out
before the FIS was recorded; making it
pre-meditated. The High Court egregiously
erred in looking at a complaint against
the I.O not produced in the trial, to find
the evidence led to be clinching insofar
as  the  culpability  of  the  accused.  A
faulty investigation cannot inure to the
benefit of the accused, but when there is
no reliable evidence, merely because the
I.O was recalcitrant or a complaint of
collusion  was  raised  against  him,  the
Court cannot presume the guilt of the
accused.  There  is  complete  lack  of
evidence  in  the  present  case  and  the
testimonies,  as  we  observed,  do  not
inspire confidence.
12. We, hence, acquit the accused and
direct that they be released forthwith if

## Page 572

any of the appellants are in custody, if
not required in any other case, and if
they were released on bail, their bail
bonds shall stand cancelled.
13.The Appeals stand allowed.”

O R D E R
This is a petition filed under Section 25 of the Code of
Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short “CPC”). The petitioner is the
wife of the respondent. The petitioner has filed this Transfer
Petition seeking the following reliefs:
“(a)  Allow the present petition and pass an order for
transfer of Petition A/1831/2024 filed under Section
9 of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 pending before learned
Family Court at Bandra, Mumbai, Maharashtra to the
learned Family Court at Ernakulum, Kerala; and
(b) Pass such other and further order/orders as this
Hon’ble Court may deem fit and proper in the facts
and circumstances of the case and in the interests of
justice.”
2. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner and
learned counsel for the respondent. 
3. Having heard learned counsel for the petitioner and
learned counsel for the respondent and on perusal of the
material on record, we find that the petitioner has made out a
case for transfer of the aforesaid petition.
4. In the result, the Transfer Petition is allowed and the
Petition A/1831/2024 titled “ Roshan  Gopalan  Nair Vs.  Shreeja
Roshan  Nair ” pending  before  the  Family  Court  at  Bandra,
Mumbai, Maharashtra is ordered to be transferred to the Family
Court at Ernakulum, Kerala.

transferee  Court  either  in-person  or  through  video
conferencing facility. If such a request is made by the
respondent herein, the Court shall make available the said
facility to him.
6. Registry to communicate this order to the transferor
Court as well as the transferee Court for taking steps in
accordance with this order. 
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

## Page 650

2. The Civil Appeal No.3132/2026 is allowed and Civil Appeal
No. 4207/2026 is dismissed  in terms of the signed reportable
judgment.
3. The  relevant  part  of  the  reportable  judgment  is  as
under:-
“15. In the peculiar circumstances of this case, we
are of the opinion that it is only proper that NOIDA
waives the penalty charges since it is neither the
default of the homebuyers nor the default of the SRA,
which led to the delay.  The homebuyers and the SRA are
sought to be penalised for past sins of the Corporate
Debtor, which cannot be allowed, especially in the
context of the authority imposing penalty, ie: the
local authority being concerned essentially with the
development of the area under its control.
16. We hence, order that in the peculiar facts and
circumstances of the case, the penalty as imposed by
the NOIDA on delay, now mulcted on the SRA and the
homebuyers, cannot be so validly imposed. We set aside
the directions to consider the time extension charges
as CIRP costs and modify the impugned order to that
extent.  NOIDA’s  appeal  praying  for  time  extension
charges even beyond the three years upto the 10th year
also stands rejected. 
17. Civil Appeal No.3132 of 2026 is allowed.
Civil Appeal No.4207 of 2026 is dismissed.” 
4. Pending application(s), if any, stands disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
applicant(s) and the learned senior counsel appearing for the
respondent(s).
3. At the outset, it was noticed that the application of the present
nature by way of clarification is being filed, which cannot be
countenanced inasmuch as this Court having passed an order would
become functus officio  and this Court in the case of ‘Supertech
Limited v. Emerald Court Owner Resident Welfare Association & Ors.”
in M.A. 1572 of 2021 in Civil Appeal No. 5041 of 2021 disposed of
04.10.2021,  has  clearly  held that such applications  seeking
clarification, modification, variation, etc., are to be nipped at the bud.
1

## Page 658

Hence, we are not inclined to entertain this Miscellaneous Application.
4. Also, in view of the order dated 28.10.2025 passed by this
Court in S.L.P. (C) No. 1634 of 2025 and Diary No. 3183 of 2025, which
is to the following effect, we are not inclined to entertain the
Miscellaneous Application.  Relevant portion thereof is reproduced as
under :
“1.Permission to file the petition in Diary No.3183/2025 is
granted.
2.Having heard learned counsel appearing for the parties,
we are not inclined to entertain these petitions. However, we
make it clear that in the event of any fresh application for
appointment by the State, is called for, the time spent by
these petitioners, from the date of joining till date of
discharge, shall be excluded for reckoning the eligibility with
regard to the age is concerned”
5. In view of the above, the Miscellaneous Application is hereby
rejected.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall  stand disposed of.

103(1), 303(2) and 352 of Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and
Section 27 of the Arms Act, 1959.
3. It is alleged that petitioners were amongst a large mob of
around  eighty  people  armed  with  deadly  weapons  that
launched  an  attack  on  the  informant  and  his  family
resulting in the death of the informant's sixteen year old
son.
4. While Petitioner No. 1 (Mainuddin) is specifically accused
of inciting the mob to violence, only general allegations
are made against Petitioner No. 2 (Nazam) & Petitioner
No. 3 (Dilshad).

5. Hence on a  prima  facie  consideration of the material on
record, we are of the opinion that the petitioner No. 2
(Nazam) & Petitioner No.3 (Dilshad) can be released on
anticipatory bail. We are not inclined to interfere insofar
as Petitioner No. 1 (Mainuddin) is concerned.
6. We order that in the event of arrest of the petitioner No.2
(Nazam) and Petitioner No.3 (Dilshad) in connection with
the offence enumerated above, they shall be released on
bail,  subject  to  such  terms  and  conditions  that  the
Investigating Officer (for short “I.O.”) may deem fit to
impose, on condition also of continued cooperation in the
investigation. 
7. Once the aforesaid petitioners are released on bail by the
I.O., on directions issued by the I.O. or summons issued by
the District & Additional Sessions Judge, IV, Araria, Bihar
(the jurisdictional court), the petitioners shall appear
before the jurisdictional court and furnish bail bonds and
ensure due appearance in the trial.
8. With the aforesaid, the petition stands disposed of.

High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior in IA 1887/2026 in CRA
95/2025,  whereby the High Court rejected the petitioner’s
fourth application for suspension of sentence during the
pendency of his appeal.
4. By Judgment dated 18.12.2024 passed by the 11th District and
Additional Sessions Judge/ Special Judge (POCSO Act), Gwalior,
Madhya Pradesh, the petitioner was convicted under Section 366
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and Sections 3 and 4 of
the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
(POCSO) Act respectively and sentenced to undergo ten years of
rigorous  imprisonment  and  a  fine  of  Rs.  10,000/-.  The
Petitioner has served more than  1 year and 10 months in
custody.  
5. Having heard learned counsel for both parties and having
perused the material on record, without expressing any final
opinion on the merits of the appeal, we are of the considered
view that a prima  facie case for suspension of sentence is
made out, given the period of custody undergone and arguable
legal issues raised regarding the information of the accused
regarding the victim’s age as represented by the victim
herself. 
6. Accordingly, the execution of the substantive sentence of
imprisonment  awarded  to  the  petitioner  in  Sessions
Case.240/2022, shall remain suspended during the pendency of
the appeal before the High Court.
7. The  learned  11th  District  and  Additional  Sessions
Judge/Special  Judge  (POCSO  Act),  Gwalior  (Jurisdictional
Court) shall release the petitioner on bail on such conditions
as deemed fit and appropriate, on the basis of the suspension

1

## Page 685

which led to registration of FIR No.70 dated 31.07.2024 under
Sections 406 and 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, registered
at Women Police Station, District Jalandhar. The petitioner is the
husband, who had applied for anticipatory bail before the High
Court, and the same prayer has been denied  vide the impugned
order.
2. The arrest of the petitioner – husband was conditionally
stayed by this Court on 29.12.2025. Thereafter, on the joint
request of the parties, the matter was referred to the Mediation
Centre attached to the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at
Chandigarh. The Mediation and Conciliation Centre of the High
Court has forwarded a Report dated 18.05.2026, duly signed by the
learned Mediator, the petitioner – husband and the wife (Manpreet
Kaur), besides one Ramesh Kumar. As per the Report, the parties
have amicably settled their matrimonial dispute(s) and as per
paragraph 10 thereof, the complainant – wife will not oppose the
grant of anticipatory bail to the petitioner – husband. They have
further resolved that a joint petition under Section 13B of the
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 for dissolution of marriage by mutual
consent shall be filed. As per the learned counsel for the
parties, the same has already been filed. The petitioner – husband
has also agreed to pay a lump-sum amount of Rs.15 lacs towards the
maintenance of the minor child, as per the details mentioned in
paragraph 8 of the Settlement Deed. 
3. The instant petition is, accordingly, disposed of in light of
the settlement between the parties and the interim bail granted to
the petitioner – husband is made absolute. The parties are well
2

## Page 686

advised to give full effect to Settlement Deed. It is clarified
that if the terms of the settlement are not complied with by the
petitioner – husband, the wife shall be at liberty to seek revival
of these proceedings.
4. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
5. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

consideration, as the time granted by this Court, vide the judgment
and order dated 22.04.2026, expired last month and we are informed
1

## Page 856

M.A. Nos. 2611-2612/2026
that the State of Tamil Nadu is yet to take necessary action.  
As already indicated in the aforestated judgment/order, any
action/inaction on the part of the State would be amenable to
redressal before the appropriate forum in accordance with law by
treating the same as a fresh cause of action.
We are, however, informed by Mr. Jayant Bhushan, learned
senior counsel, appearing for some of the parties in the special
leave petition(s), that basic amenities have not been provided to
the occupants of the apartments constructed on the lands in
question.  
Learned counsel appearing for the State of Tamil Nadu states
that she has no instructions in that regard.
We need to only flag this issue, as there was a direction to
the State to address the plight of such occupants.
Subject  to  the  above  observation,  the  miscellaneous
applications are dismissed.
We reiterate the liberty recorded in paragraph 25 of the
judgment  and  order  dated  22.04.2026  with  regard  to  seeking
redressal of grievances, if any, before the appropriate forum in
accordance with law.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This Special Leave Petition seeks to impugn an interim
order passed by the High Court on an appeal preferred by the
petitioner against the award passed by the Motor Accident
Claims Tribunal (“the Tribunal”).
2. The High Court has entertained the appeal and stayed the
award amount subject to deposit of the entire amount. The
High Court has further directed that 50 per cent of the
1

## Page 878

deposited amount shall be invested in a fixed deposit, and
the balance 50 per cent shall be allowed to be withdrawn by
the claimants.
3. The grievance of the petitioner is that the High Court
ought not to have allowed withdrawal of the deposited amount
without requiring the claimants to furnish security.
4. We have perused the order passed by the Tribunal. A
perusal thereof would reveal that there is no serious issue
on the factum of accident and its resultant effect; further,
issue  No.  3  related  to  the  aspect  as  to  whether  the
offending vehicle was insured with the petitioner; and the
other relevant issue was whether the driver of the offending
vehicle held a valid driving license. Both these issues were
decided against the petitioner.
5. In such circumstances, we do not find a good reason to
interfere with the impugned order.
6. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, dismissed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
8. However, we make it clear that any observation made
herein above shall not be considered as an opinion expressed
by us on the merits of the appeal pending before the High
Court.  The High Court shall proceed to decide the appeal
uninfluenced by any of the observations made herein above. 
   
(CHETAN ARORA)                                  (SAPNA BANSAL)

1. The submission on behalf of the petitioners is
that for seeking the benefit of Section 60(b) of the
Indian Easements Act, 1882 (“the 1882 Act”), the
licensee  must  act  upon  the  license  and  raise
constructions  or  execute  work  of  a  permanent
character and incur expenses in its execution /
completion.
1

## Page 880

2. In paragraph 53 of the impugned judgment, the
High Court accepts the position that the petitioners
(defendants)  have  raised  constructions  of  a
permanent nature. The High Court in paragraph 55 of
the  impugned  judgment  declined  the  benefit  of
Section 60(b) of the 1882 Act only on the ground
that the defendants in their written statements have
denied relationship of licensor and licensee. 
3. It has been submitted that the relationship of
licensor and licensee is set up by the plaintiff
himself, therefore once it was found that occupation
of the defendant was as a licensee of the plaintiff
and constructions of a permanent nature were raised
by the defendant, without any resistance from the
plaintiff, the benefit of Section 60(b) of the 1882
Act could not have been denied.
4. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.
5. In the meantime, execution of the decree shall
remain stayed.

CORAM    HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANOJ MISRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Shivam Prashar, Adv.
                   Mr. Amol Chitravanshi, AOR
                                      
For Respondent(s)  Mr. Divyanshu Kumar Srivastava, AOR
                   Ms. Rasika Jalan, Adv.
                   Mr. Shivam Nagpal, Adv.
                             
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. This Special Leave Petition seeks to question the
order passed by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh at
Shimla  dated  25.09.2025  whereby  the  petition  of  the
petitioner seeking quashing of the order passed by the
learned  Special  Judge-I,  Shimla,  dated  26.07.2025,
rejecting prayer for discharge, has been dismissed.
3. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that
though FIR refers to the name of the petitioner amongst
other accused in the subject column, but in the contents
1

## Page 886

of  the  FIR,  there  are  no  allegations  against  the
petitioner. It has also been submitted that statement of
the victim is also silent in respect of the involvement of
the petitioner except that the petitioner had refused to
let her tie Rakhi on the ground that she was of a lower
caste.
4. We have carefully gone through the materials available
on  record  including  the  police  report  and  the
supplementary police report as well as the order passed by
the High Court. A perusal thereof would reveal that the
investigating officer, while submitting the police report,
has placed reliance on statement of one witness, namely,
Bhupinder, who has made allegations against the petitioner
of hurling caste abuses at the victim. Once such is the
position, it cannot be said that there is no material
against the petitioner.
5. As to what offences the petitioner should be charged
with, would be determined at the time of framing of
charge.
6. In such circumstances, we do not find any error in
rejection of the discharge application.
7. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, dismissed.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.       
(CHETAN ARORA)                                  (SAPNA BANSAL)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Whether the phrase “other experiences” in a
University affiliated college would enure to the
benefit of the petitioner is the matter in issue. 
2. The  candidature  of  the  petitioner  was  not
considered for additional 5 marks on the ground that
the experience was in a private institution named,
Metropolitan Homeopathic Medical Collage & Hospital,
1

## Page 890

which was not affiliated to the Government.
3. The submission on behalf of the petitioner is
that the said college was affiliated to the West
Bengal University of Health Sciences. Colleges for
imparting degree / courses need to be affiliated to
a university, and therefore, experience in a college
affiliated to the University is sufficient for award
of additional marks.
4. Before we proceed to adjudicate, it would be
appropriate  for  us  to  call  for  the  relevant
statutory provisions applicable in the State of West
Bengal qua affiliation of a college.
5. In this regard, the learned counsel for the
parties pray for and are allowed two weeks’ time to
file relevant rules or statutes.
6. List immediately after expiry of two weeks.

1. The present petition is arising out of order dated 24.04.2026
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras, dismissing the
Writ Petition filed by the petitioner upholding the State Human
Rights Commission’s recommendation for compensation and monetary
recovery from the Officers and disciplinary action against them.
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner has argued before this
Court that there is no evidence on the basis of which the State
Human Rights Commission has submitted the report.
3. This Court has carefully gone through the aforesaid report and
is of the considered opinion that the State Human Rights Commission
was  justified  in  directing  departmental  enquiry  against  the

## Page 900

Officers in question.

concerned, the amount of Rs. 2,90,000/- (Rupees Two Lakh and Ninety
Thousand only), as informed, has already been paid.
5. The State Human Rights Commission has also held that the amount,
after payment to the respondent should be recovered from the
Officers in question.
6. We make it clear that the recovery from Officers in question
shall be subject to the outcome of the departmental enquiry which
the officers are going to face now.  With the aforesaid, the
petition stands disposed of.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL)…………………. Diary No(s). 38854/2026
INDRAKALA JOGINDER NANDA & ORS.                    Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT BOMBAY & ORS.          Respondent(s)
IA No. 251353/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN REFILING/CURING THE
DEFECTS
 
Date : 31-08-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Basant R, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Amol Nirmalkumar Suryawanshi, AOR
                   Ms. Damini Vishwakarma, Adv.
                   Mr. B Dhananjay, Adv.
                   Mr. Raunak Arora, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. In this petition, filed under Article 32 of the Constitution
of India, the petitioners, who are Presiding Officers of various
Family Courts in Maharashtra, seek a declaration that the office of
a Judge of a Family Court constitutes a “judicial office” within
the meaning of Article 217(2)(a), thereby rendering them eligible
for consideration for appointment as Judges of a High Court.
Pertinently, this precise question was considered by this Court and
answered against similarly situated Family Court Judges in  S.D.
Joshi and others v. High Court of Judicature at Bombay and others ,
1

## Page 1048

(2011) 1 SCC 252. The present writ petition, therefore, seeks, in
substance, reconsideration of that settled decision.
3. At the outset, it appears that a writ petition under Article
32 cannot be employed as a means of seeking reconsideration of a
binding judgment of this Court or as a substitute for the remedies
available against such a judgment. Even otherwise, the petitioners
have not demonstrated any change in the governing constitutional or
statutory framework that would warrant taking a view different from
that expressed in S.D. Joshi (supra).
4. Contrarily, it seems to us that the only recourse that might
be available to the petitioners would be to impress upon the
jurisdictional High Court and the State Government to reformulate
the rules re: appointment of Presiding Officers of Family Courts,
essentially in light of the provisions for such appointment as is
prevailing in other States. We hasten to add that this would
essentially be a policy matter for which the High Court and State
Government,  in  consultation  with  each  other,  may  take  an
appropriate decision. We express no opinion in that regard.
5. The Writ Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
6. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR
2

For Petitioner(s): Mr. Siddharth Mittal, AOR

For Respondent(s): 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner(s).
2. Petitioner(s) are aggrieved by an order passed by
the  High  Court  rejecting  their  revision  petition
assailing  the  order  of  the  Trial  Court  whereby
respondents-plaintiffs’ prayer for amendment of plaint
was allowed.
1

## Page 1082

3. Relevant portion of the impugned order reads thus:
“6.Moreover, a perusal of the original plaint
shows  that  the  foundational  pleadings  with
respect to the nature and ownership of subject
land were already in existence. By way of the
proposed amendment, the plaintiffs have merely
sought to incorporate an additional relief of
declaration based on the same set of facts. In
such circumstances, the amendment sought for
neither changes the cause of action; nor alters
the nature and character of the suit. Rather,
it is necessary for the proper and effective
adjudication  of  the  dispute  between  the
parties. In view of the above, the impugned
order passed by the learned trial Court does
not suffer from any illegality or perversity
warranting  interference  in  exercise  of
revisional jurisdiction.”
4. In view of the above, we do not find any good
ground to entertain the Special Leave Petition.
5. Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  is
dismissed.
6. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

1. Respondent was prosecuted for offences under Sections 313,
376(2)(n), 493 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,
‘IPC’). However, the learned Sessions Court vide the judgment and
order dated 18.08.2023 acquitted the respondent.
2. The State did not file appeal against such acquittal. On the
other hand, the petitioner-informant filed Criminal Appeal No.320
of 2023 before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana (briefly the
‘High Court’ hereinafter). By the impugned judgment and order dated
20.01.2026, the aforesaid appeal came to be dismissed.

3. We have perused the evidence on record and the conclusions
reached  by  both  the  courts  below.  It  is  a  confirmation  of
acquittal.

case where the acquittal by the Trial Court has been affirmed by
the High Court, we are not inclined to entertain the Special Leave
Petition.
5. The same is accordingly dismissed.

date of birth as 01.05.1962. In the year
2015, the respondent applied for change in
the date of birth on the basis of a school

2
leaving certificate showing his date of birth
as 01.07.1968, which was coincidentally the
date of birth recorded in the EPF record.

petition in the year 2020 seeking change of
date of birth in the service record.
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner
would submit that if the petitioner’s date of
birth  is  taken  as  01.07.1968  then,  the
respondent would be only 14 years of age at
the time when he joined the service as a
daily wager, which is impermissible.

stay on the impugned order passed by the High

Date : 02-09-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR
For Petitioner(s) : 
                   Mr. Rajesh Srivastava, AOR
                   Mr. Rahul Kumar, Adv.
                   Mr. Anil Kumar Gaur, Adv.
                   Mrs. Deepika Singh, Adv.
                   Ms. Riddhi Gupta, Adv.                          
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Issue notice limited to the extent
of examining the issue as to whether this
Court can exercise powers under Article 142
of the Constitution of India to direct the
insurer to pay and recover, as the insurer is
not liable to pay the liability or otherwise,
in the case of a gratuitous passenger.

## Page 1124

2
3. In  the  matters  of  N  ational  
Insurance Company Limited vs. Baljit Kaur &
others, reported in (2004) 2 SCC 1, National
Insurance Company vs. Saju P.Paul & another,
reported  in  (2013)  2  SCC  41  and  Manuara
Khatun & others vs. Rajesh Kumar Singh &
others, reported in (2017) 4 SCC 796 and 2025
INSC 867, 2025 SCC Online SC 2297 and (2009)
8 SCC 785 , this Court has exercised powers
under  Article  142  of  the  Constitution  of
India,  however,  in  the  case  of  National
Insurance  Company  Ltd.  vs.  Parvathneni,
(2018) 9 SCC 657 , the issue as to whether
this Court can invoke powers under Article
142 of the Constitution of India in a  case
relating to a gratuitous passenger, has been
kept open.
4. Issue  notice,  returnable  on
02.11.2026.

solely on the ground that the petitioner has an alternative

the appellate authority, in accordance with law.

a statutory appeal.

own merits, without being influenced in any manner by any
of the observations made by the High Court in its impugned
judgment and order.

dismissed.

Rajasthan.

weeks from date. Such affidavit ought to include,  inter  alia , the following
particulars:
(i)  chargesheet, if filed;

## Page 1284

(ii) number of witnesses proposed to be examined by the
prosecution;

therefor;

examined;
(vi) criminal antecedents of the petitioner;
(vii) whether any co-accused is enlarged on bail; and
(viii) any other information relevant for a decision on the
special leave petition.
4. Rejoinder thereto, if any, may be filed by a week thereafter.
5. List the instant special leave petition immediately after S.L.P. (Crl.)
No.15822/2026 on the next date of hearing i.e., 05 th October, 2026, as both
special leave petitions challenge the common impugned judgment and order
dated 13th August, 2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at

case FIR registered by the Central Bureau of Intelligence

petitioner stating that he has never been arrested in the
CBI case and no order of remand has been passed in respect
of the petitioner in the CBI case, therefore, there has
been no occasion for the petitioner to move the Competent
Court for grant of bail in the said matter.

as a party respondent in this Special Leave Petition.

are of the view that no case is made out for suspension of
the substantive order of sentence of life imprisonment.

petitioner- convict is undergoing sentence past more than 12
years. His appeal is of the year 2021.

give some priority to Criminal Appeal No. 628 of 2021 and see
to it that the same is heard and disposed of within a period
of six months from today.

High Court of Judicature of Rajasthan in  S.B. Criminal 3rd
Misc Suspension of Sentence Application (Appeal) No.219/2026
in SB Criminal Appeal No.1707/2025 , whereby the High Court
rejected the petitioner’s third application for suspension of
sentence during the pendency of their appeal.
4. By Judgment dated 23.06.2025 passed by Additional Sessions
Judge No. 2, Ajmer, Rajasthan the Petitioner was convicted
under Sections 307, 341, 323, 452 read with Section 34 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and sentenced him to undergo
seven years of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs.55,000/-.
The Petitioner has served more than 1 year and 3 months  in
judicial custody. 
5. Having heard learned counsel for both parties and having
perused the material on record, without expressing any final
opinion on the merits of the appeal, we are of the considered
view that a prima facie case for suspension of sentence is
made out, given the period of custody undergone, and arguable
legal issues raised in appeal. 
6. Accordingly, the execution of the substantive sentence of 
Imprisonment  awarded  to  the  petitioner  in  Sessions  Case
No.10/2013(CIS No.360/2014) in  PS Civil Line, Ajmer  shall
remain suspended during the pendency of the appeal before the
High Court.
7. The  learned  Additional  Sessions  Judge  No.2,  Ajmer
(Jurisdictional Court) shall release the petitioner on bail on
such conditions as deemed fit and appropriate, on the basis of
the suspension of sentence granted by us. In the event of
breach of any conditions specified, it shall be open to the
State to move an application before the Jurisdictional Court
for cancellation of bail.
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the above terms.
